In this warm and wide-ranging episode of Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams, Kirk welcomes Rachel Antoine, Senior Director of International Operations at Braille Institute, for a conversation about Braille literacy and the programs that sustain it. Kirk opens with his own Braille history, losing his sight at five, learning to read and write Braille from Mrs. Summers at the Oregon State School for the Blind, and depending on Braille books through long hospital stays, then traces his three encounters with Braille Challenge: a regional in Tampa, a 2019 keynote at the Braille Challenge gala, and a return visit in 2026 where he met Rachel. Rachel explains that Braille Challenge has grown from one Southern California regional in 2000 to over 80 regionals worldwide, reaching around 2,200 students a year and over 26,000 since it began, with the competition as the vehicle and Braille literacy as the mission.

The second half covers the documentary Brailled It, filmed at the 2024 Braille Challenge Finals with GoPros worn by competitors Salome, Isaiah and Christopher Morgan and now touring US cinemas; the program’s first African regional in Kenya, where more than 1,000 students took part and many competed with slate and stylus because there were not enough Braillers to go round; and plans to build an East Africa model spanning Uganda and Tanzania, with three Kenyan students due at the 2027 Finals. Rachel also describes the free, non-competitive foundational category any parent, teacher or grandparent can order year-round, and Cane Quest, Braille Institute’s orientation and mobility program, whose SoCal regional runs October 3rd at the Los Angeles Zoo.

TRANSCRIPT:

Podcast Commentator: Welcome to Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams, where we bring you powerful conversations with leading voices in disability rights, employment and inclusion. Our guests share their expertise, experiences and strategies to inspire action and create a more inclusive world. If you’re passionate about social justice or want to make a difference, you’re in the right place. Let’s dive in with your host, Dr. Kirk Adams.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Welcome, everybody, to another episode of Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams. I am that Dr. Kirk Adams, talking to you from my home office in Seattle, Washington. And very excited today, because we’re going to be talking a lot about Braille. I have Rachel Antoine here with me from the Braille Institute. Say hey, Rachel.

Rachel Antoine: Hello. So happy to be here. Thank you, Dr. Adams.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And Rachel, what’s your title at Braille?

Rachel Antoine: Yeah. So I am Senior Director of International Operations at Braille Institute. My role is really about connecting programs, people and possibilities around the world. I lead our international work, expanding programs like Braille Challenge and Cane Quest, and building partnerships with organizations, schools, and educators in other countries.

Dr. Kirk Adams: That sounds like a fun job to me.

Rachel Antoine: It is.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So my history with Braille — I think many of you know I’m a blind person. My retinas detached when I was five years old. I was in kindergarten in Lynnwood, Washington, north of Seattle. My parents — I was born when they were in college, so they were in their mid-20s when my retinas detached. They had never met a blind person before. Before I became one very quickly. And they were told that I wasn’t going to be allowed to come back to the neighborhood school, that I needed to go to the school for blind children. At that time, the model was, I think, most blind and deaf kids went to a state school. My parents visited the Washington State school. They did not like what they saw as far as the level of academic activity. My retinal surgeon was in Oregon, and someone there at University of Oregon Medical Hospital said the Oregon State School for the Blind is awesome. So I remember visiting there, and they agreed that it was awesome. And they quit their jobs and moved the family down to Oregon so I could go to the Oregon State School. And I had a teacher named Mrs. Summers for first, second and third grade. May she rest in peace. And whenever I’m in a setting where they say, name the person who had the most influence on your life, I say, Mrs. Summers, because she taught me how to read and write Braille.

Dr. Kirk Adams: I was hospitalized a lot. I had quite a number of eye surgeries that were painful and unsuccessful, and I would spend 10 to 14 days after each surgery in the hospital with my head in a clamp, so I couldn’t move my head to disrupt the surgery they’d done. So Braille was really my lifeline. And my mom would go to the Braille library of the National Library Service library in Salem and load up the station wagon with boxes of books and bring them to the hospital. And I read and read and read. So Braille has been super important to me. I learned about the Braille Challenge, gosh, ten, 12, 14 years ago. I was aware of it. At the time, I was the CEO of the Lighthouse for the Blind here in Seattle. And we had a mentor-protegé relationship with the Lighthouse for the Blind in Port Richey, Florida, which is near Tarpon Springs, the sponge capital of the United States, which is fairly near Tampa. And the Tampa Lighthouse was having the regional Braille Challenge the week that I was there. So my wife, Ros, and I went, and I got to meet the kids and see the activities they were doing. It was a Harry Potter theme, so it must have been when the Harry Potter books were so popular. And I had a chance to talk to the parents while the kids were doing their activities.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And like my parents, most of them had never met a blind person before. They had a blind child. So they had a lot of questions about how to raise a child successfully who is blind. So we talked about being developmentally appropriate, and talked about creating a Braille-rich environment — that your sighted child is surrounded by print all the time. The cereal box, the magazine on the table, the street signs you drive by. And you have to be very intentional with the young blind child to have lots of Braille around. And I said, order some Braille magazines from the National Library Service, and let them play with those and tear them up, chew on them and do what little kids do with board books. And put Braille on everything, label everything with Braille. And then, if your four-year-old sighted child is out playing in the sandbox and tussling with other kids over the toys, you want your blind child out on that playground with their cane doing the same thing. If your 12- or 13-year-old sighted child is taking the bus or getting themselves downtown to meet friends, to do things, go to movies, you need to make sure your blind child is learning how to use public transportation and has orientation and mobility skills, so they can do those same things.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And we talked about the school-to-work transition. You have sighted kids doing chores. Blind kids need to do chores, and you need to figure out different approaches to do things. But you want blind kids doing the same thing sighted kids do, using the alternative techniques of blindness. And literacy is so important. Braille is so important. For me, there was no question — I was totally blind. So in first grade, I learned Braille. Blindness comes in so many variations. Many people who are legally blind have some usable vision. Sometimes there’s questions whether or not kids need to learn Braille. And I always say, if the visually impaired child cannot read at the same speed and comprehension as a sighted child, if they’re trying to use magnification, they need to learn Braille. Braille is literacy. I say, if listening to materials is sufficient, then why do sighted people still read? So we need to read too. So anyway, I did the Braille Challenge regional in Tampa, and I was given a certificate of Braille wizardry, which I still have, with the Harry Potter theme. And then, my gosh, five, six years later, I became the president and CEO of the American Foundation for the Blind. And I was visiting partners around the country, and I made a stop at the Braille Institute and sat with — that was before your time, Rachel.

Dr. Kirk Adams: 2016, 2017. Yeah. And got to know folks. And then I got a call in early 2019 asking if I would come and give the keynote talk at the Braille Challenge gala. So again, my wife, Ros, and I flew out and met the kids. And they — [unclear 00:08:13] Rachel will tell you all about this — but they fly in the winners from the regions, and they gather on the USC campus. And [I] remember the Trojan, the hated Trojan marching band — I’m a Husky fan — marched the kids across the campus playing the USC fight song. And they had their competitions, and then the awards gala. And I got to talk about how important Braille is to me, and said a lot of the things I’ve said so far on this podcast, in a more organized and elegant fashion. But I talked about the importance of Braille and how meaningful it was to be there. They had an alumni who’s become a really good friend of mine, a young lady named Caitlin Hernandez, who’s totally blind. She lives in San Francisco, and she’s a public school teacher. And she gave the alumni speech, and it was just such a moving experience.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And then fast forward to this year, 2026. I was talking to Dimitri Kales, who’s now the CEO of Braille Institute, and we were just catching up and comparing notes on a few things. And he said, well, next time you’re going to be in the Los Angeles area, let me know. I said, I’m going to be there next week, because my wife and I are visiting our daughter Rachel, who lives in Highland Park. We’re coming to visit her. And he said, well, Braille Challenge is next Saturday. I’d love for you and your wife and daughter to be our guests. So we attended again — a beautiful alumni speaker, a great keynote speaker. The kids were so excited to win their awards. And afterwards our daughter Rachel said, I want you to meet Rachel Antoine. So that’s when I met Rachel Antoine. And I’ve been so excited about your vision for the future of Braille Challenge. Another good friend of mine, Stephanie Jones, was there from the Clovernook Center, and they’re out of Cincinnati. They’re doing wonderful work with you in Kenya.

Dr. Kirk Adams: They showed a preview of a documentary called Brailled It, where some of the competitors were given cameras and filmed, and they’ve made a documentary which is now airing around the country. So the Braille Challenge is on the move and expanding under your leadership. And I just am so pleased to get to know you and to have you here, and just love to hear you give more detail about Braille Challenge and Cane Quest and whatever you would like to share with the good people listening.

Rachel Antoine: Awesome. Thank you so much, Dr. Adams. That was such a beautiful summary. So as you mentioned, Braille still matters. We’re seeing a decline in Braille literacy and, in many places, a decline in opportunities for students to receive Braille instruction. And internationally, there are additional challenges like limited research, fewer educators, limited resources, and inconsistent access to Braille materials and technology. But technology doesn’t replace literacy. Braille is still essential for learning spelling, grammar, punctuation, written communication, proofreading, and independent reading. So technology gives you access to information, but Braille gives you that literacy. Braille is a lifelong skill, and that is what makes Braille Challenge so powerful. Braille Challenge was born in the year 2000 as an arena for blind students to participate in an academic competition, the only one of its kind. But Braille Challenge is much more than a competition. The competition is the vehicle, but Braille literacy is the mission. It gives students a reason to practice their Braille skills in something meaningful to work towards. It gives them a sense of belonging among their peers, a sense of community. They’re not just learning Braille, they’re using Braille. So over the past 26 years, Braille Challenge has grown from one regional competition in Southern California to over 80 regionals across the globe. In each season, students step up to the challenge in 38 US states, Canada, the UK, Australia, Ireland, and most recently, this past spring, Kenya. And I attended the Kenya regional. It was amazing. I’ll chat about that as well.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Awesome.

Rachel Antoine: Yeah. And later this year, several schools in India will be participating in Braille Challenge for the very first time. And all of this is provided at no cost to each and every participant.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And so it is a skills competition, right? So it is reading Braille, writing Braille, spelling. And blind people who don’t read Braille, who listen to everything, are terrible spellers. So I’m glad to see spelling. And then I think there’s something about graphics, about understanding tactile graphics. So could you tell a little bit about the nuts and bolts of what these young people go through as far as the various competitions they do?

Rachel Antoine: For sure. So students are practicing reading comp, spelling, speed and accuracy — which is them listening to an audio file and doing formatting — and then proofreading, where they’re reading a document and finding all the errors, and then tactile graphs. So they’re reading a map, a chart, a cell, anything like that. So they’re really using Braille. They’re really getting their hands on Braille. And there are not enough opportunities in the classroom for teachers to provide Braille materials. So teachers are really eager to join our program and get their hands on free Braille materials, free charts and graphs. And we’re just really happy to provide all these teachers with these materials.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So with the 80 regionals, how many total? It’s K through 12, right?

Rachel Antoine: Yes, yes.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yeah. So with 80 regionals, about how many kids roughly participated this year?

Rachel Antoine: Yeah. So in 2026, we had around 2,200 kids participate, and annually it’s around that. It’s going up with our larger international regionals. But since the year 2000, we’ve had over 26,000 students take on the Braille Challenge. So that’s a really large number. And we’re impacting lots of students around the globe. But there’s so many more blind students than 26,000. So we want to reach all the schools for the blind and find these students where they are, to give them access to Braille Challenge.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So tell me a little bit about your background. What brought you to Braille Institute?

Rachel Antoine: Sure. Yeah. So I’m originally from Boston. Go Celtics, go Patriots, Red Sox. But I started at the Mass Commission for the Blind as a program manager. And I knew I always wanted to move to California. I love SoCal. I was tired of the snow. So I found an opportunity at Braille Institute, and I’ve always been in our — we used to be called National Programs, now we’re called International Operations. So I’ve always worked on the Braille Challenge program, in addition to Cane Quest. And I did a little bit of work with our youth programs as well. But Braille Challenge has always been home for me.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yeah. Did you have exposure to blindness as a young person? What brought you originally to the Massachusetts Commission for the Blind?

Rachel Antoine: I was working in state government, and I was working at the Division of Professional Licensure. I was doing all the background checks, and when they heard from me, they were getting the bad news, because they had to go in for a hearing, I needed additional information. So it was really making a lot of tough phone calls. And I [said to] myself, I need to do something more. I need to do something more meaningful. I want to work with — I want happy news. Yeah. So I found a role at the Mass Commission for the Blind, and then just fell in love with the community. What a powerful community. And the students, the adults — it’s just been great to work with this community. So ever since the Commission for the Blind, now at Braille Institute — yeah, this community has become home for me, so I really enjoy it.

Dr. Kirk Adams: All right. So when I was there in 2019, I met a young man who was probably 11 years old named Christopher Morgan.

Rachel Antoine: Oh, yeah.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And he very, very authentically believed in his bones he was going to be the first blind NBA player, and he was doing some stuff with the Atlanta Hawks. And Ros and I had a nice time, sat with his mom. And then lo and behold, 2026, there he is, all grown up, heading off to college, his final year with Braille Challenge and, of course, winning again. And he is one of the three main competitors who did the filming that has become the Brailled It documentary.

Rachel Antoine: Yes.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And I had David Grabias, one of the producers of the documentary, and Christopher on this very same podcast.

Rachel Antoine: Oh, wonderful.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Seven weeks ago. And Christopher said that as he matured and became a teenager, he did come to realize that he probably would not be the first blind NBA player, but that he could be a world-class athlete. So he threw himself wholeheartedly into the sport of goalball, which was designed for us. And he is the youngest member of the US men’s goalball team. So we talked about that. And so Brailled It is being screened around the country. There’s a screening in Seattle. I know there’s one at Library of Congress. I saw a trailer. I haven’t seen the documentary yet. About the time this podcast airs, I’ll be at the Seattle screening. So I’m very excited about that. I sat at a table this year with one of the other three main folks, Isaiah, who is a avid hockey fan from Canada. And when we first came up, I was greeted by a young lady named Salome, also the third of the trio. And Salome, very friendly, very charismatic, said, I want to get in there because I care about eating and I care about winning. She did eat and she did win.

Rachel Antoine: So I love that.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Oh, it was good. So could you tell us a little bit more about the documentary and how that came to be, and what people know about that?

Rachel Antoine: Of course. Oh, I am just smiling from ear to ear talking about it. My colleague Madeline Hernandez just spoke at the Library of Congress yesterday. There was a screening of it there in front of congressmen and women and lots of powerful people in DC. So just kudos to Madeline, Lisa Lepore and Brian Sheridan, who represented Braille Institute yesterday. But Brailled It is such a powerful film, because it puts blind people at the center of their own stories. It showcases the creativity, talent and lived experience of blind youth, while challenging some of the assumptions many may have about blindness. And then all this happens around Braille Challenge. So Braille Challenge creates an opportunity. It celebrates the talent of these Braille readers. And Brailled It makes sure that these youth have the platform to be seen, heard, and recognized for what they do, not just for being blind. So Brailled It was filmed at our 2024 Braille Challenge Finals. Salome, Isaiah, and Christopher were picked to star in the film. And it just authentically showcases their day to day as they’re going through the program. We have a three-day weekend where we bring the students out from all over the world, and we highlight them at the second tier of the program at our Braille Challenge Finals. And it’s a culmination of the Braille Challenge experience. Students around the world spend months preparing, competing at regionals and building their skills, and then those top students come together at finals.

Rachel Antoine: So it’s not just a competition. It’s a celebration of Braille literacy, achievement, confidence, and community. And then those three kiddos had GoPros to capture their first-hand experience throughout the program. So it’s so fun. It’s hilarious, it’s sweet, it’s heartwarming. There’s something for the kids, for the parents, for the siblings. You find yourself in every one of these characters in the movie. So it’s just really powerful. And it’s screening all across the US. It’s at film festivals, in the film festival circuit. I’ll be going up to San Francisco this weekend to see it at the Roxie Theater in SF. And it’s screening in Seattle. It’s screening in Atlanta. It was just screening in New York City, DC yesterday, in LA all next week starting this Friday. So we are just really, really excited to bring this film to new audiences, and to change the assumption about blindness. One of the most exciting parts of the film — it reminds us that access isn’t just about providing a service or a tool, it’s about creating an opportunity for people to participate, create, compete, lead, and to tell their own stories. So that’s really what it is about, and I’m just so happy to be a part of it.

Dr. Kirk Adams: I’m looking forward to it. I remember at the gala this year, we all gave a hearty one, two, three — Brailled It!

Rachel Antoine: Oh yes.

Dr. Kirk Adams: That was fun. Yeah. How — if someone’s listening and they know a blind person K through 12 who would benefit from more focus and exposure to Braille and connecting with other blind kids… After third grade, after I finished at the school for the blind, I was the only blind student in all of my schools from fourth grade through my PhD. Really. So I was never around any other blind kids. So I could just feel the connection and the friendliness, and the kids rooting for each other and clapping for each other. And that was such a sense of camaraderie. I was very happy for them. I was a little melancholy that I didn’t have those experiences as a blind kid. But I’m sure glad they were having that, thanks to the Braille Challenge. Thank you. So if someone listening is a blind kid, knows a blind kid, or is an adult who wants to support Braille Challenge in some way, how do people get involved and get engaged?

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely. So help us bring Braille Challenge to your community. It might already be there. There might be a regional near you. If you check out our website, https://www.braillechallenge.org, you’ll be able to see our list of regionals. So we have regionals all over the world, but we want to grow. If you don’t see a regional in your community, reach out to us at braillechallenge@brailleinstitute.org. That’s our email address. And let’s have a conversation. Get your students involved. Get your youth involved. Braille Challenge looks very different all over the world. We have regionals that are ten students, 20 students. And then we have the Kenya regional — that’s a thousand students, and we’re aiming to make it 2,000 students. So no matter the size, you can bring Braille Challenge to you. We also have our foundational category, which is a non-competitive category for students — early Braille learning, Braille immersion. And you can order those materials any time of the year. And that is Braille Challenge. So we want these students to be part of a community. As you mentioned, a lot of these kids are the only blind students in their school. But when they come to Braille Challenge, they’re part of a community, and they’re celebrated, and they realize that they’re not alone.

Rachel Antoine: So we want—

Dr. Kirk Adams: Tell me more about the — did you say foundational series? Okay. Tell me. So you can order materials and they’re sent to you. It’s not part of the competition.

Rachel Antoine: Oh, yeah.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So what do the families receive?

Rachel Antoine: Yeah. So our foundational category is for Braille immersion, early Braille learning skills. And this is non-competitive. So you receive charts and graphs, spelling and proofreading or reading comp. And then you can go on our website and order, and we will send you those materials year round. So we do have [a] specific timeline for Braille Challenge season, in order to be eligible for finals. But foundational — you can order these documents year round. If you’re a parent, if you’re a teacher, if you’re a grandparent, and you want your grandchild to have more Braille materials, feel free to order them through us, and they will always be free of charge. And we look forward to getting more Braille in the hands of your students.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yes, yes. So as I talked [about] earlier, at the beginning — to create that Braille-rich environment for blind kids, so they have the same amount of exposure that sighted kids have to print.

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So you go to https://braillechallenge.org, order those foundational materials, give them to the blind kid in your life, please. Okay. So glad that you — I didn’t realize that that was available.

Rachel Antoine: Oh, yeah.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And then should we talk about Cane Quest, too?

Rachel Antoine: Sure. Yeah. Or can I make one more?

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yeah. Please. You can do whatever you want.

Rachel Antoine: Thank you so much. So we want to get Braille Challenge into organizations and students around the world who need it. So Kenya has been a really exciting part of Braille Challenge’s international growth. In 2026, we launched our first Braille Challenge program in Kenya, and it was also our first regional competition on the African continent. We partnered with Clovernook, who was already doing important work in Kenya, and the response was incredible. More than 1,000 students participated, along with 200-plus educators across three schools and 16 partner organizations. These students were celebrated for their Braille skills. They build confidence. It wasn’t just a competition. We were bringing together educators, teachers, building skills and creating more awareness around the importance of Braille literacy. So this was really felt and powerful across the country. And what’s next? So we’re looking at year two already, with plans to expand beyond Kenya and building an East Africa model that includes Uganda and Tanzania. So two additional countries. And the goal is to reach 2,000 students and over 300 educators and coordinators, continuing to build that local leadership. And then one of the most exciting parts of this program is that three Kenyan students will be joining us at Braille Challenge Finals in 2027.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Nice.

Rachel Antoine: Yes. So for these students, this is an incredible opportunity to meet other Braille readers from around the world, to experience Braille Challenge Finals firsthand, and to see themselves as part of a larger global Braille community. And what makes this work so meaningful is that it started as a regional competition in Kenya, but it’s now creating a pathway for students to participate on an international stage. So they’re not just coming to compete, they’re coming to show what’s possible. And it’s just so powerful. It’s powerful.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Okay. 2,000 kids in Africa will be participating [in] Braille Challenge 2027. That is tremendous.

Rachel Antoine: And I attended that regional in person. I was in Kenya for three weeks, working with those students, getting to know the educators, setting up the contest rooms, the classrooms across the campuses. So it was really powerful. And I can’t wait to go back for year two. Hopefully it’s in May of ’27. Yeah, we’re looking for support to join us on that trip and to help us make this possible again. So please do not hesitate to reach out.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So you mentioned earlier international Braille and lack of resources and materials and technology. So were there Perkins Braillers going, or were—? How’s the resource situation for kids learning Braille in Kenya?

Rachel Antoine: Yeah. Kenya really was the model for what an international Braille Challenge can look like. Resources, they were lacking. There weren’t enough Braillers for every student. Lots of students competed using our slate and stylus, which we haven’t seen before. But they’re showing what’s possible. When we add more Braille Challenge across the world, we’re not just trying to add countries to a map. We’re trying to build a global ecosystem for Braille literacy that is locally led and sustainable. And the ultimate goal is for communities to have the people, the training, the partnerships, and the resources they need to continue the work long after our initial investment. So year one in Kenya proved that demand. Year two is about building that capacity, getting them more resources. So that’s what we’re working on — getting those students more Braillers, getting more slate and stylus. Some students prefer slate and stylus.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Well, I learned how to use a slate and stylus when I was six. And I carry one in my briefcase because the refreshable Braille display tablet doesn’t work.

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So I greatly appreciate the slate and stylus, which, for those of you who don’t know, is a method of writing Braille by hand with a stylus that pokes out the dot from the back side. So you need to learn to write right to left, and reversing each of your Braille characters. It’s a bit of an art. But I love that our kids [are] using slate and stylus. So I assume you would accept a donation, if anyone listening wants to donate and designate their gift to support the Braille Challenge.

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely, absolutely. The need is so great out there in Kenya, and our regionals domestically, and just all over the world. Yeah, we want to be able to do this program wherever it’s needed. We want to meet the students where they are. So your donation will make a difference. Sharing the word, sharing some of our posts, following us on LinkedIn and Facebook, and getting involved. We really would love your support in making sure Braille literacy is here to stay. With technology everywhere you look — and it’s a good thing as well — but technology and Braille can work together. And Braille Challenge is all about that.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Well, I have a slate and stylus in my bag. I have a Perkins Brailler right here. I have a [unclear 00:31:43]-character Braille display attached to my laptop in front of me. I’ve got a Braille tablet, Android-based tablet, with 32-character refreshable Braille on my lap. Got a Braille embosser sitting right behind me.

Rachel Antoine: Amazing.

Dr. Kirk Adams: And when I did my doctoral work — I have my PhD in leadership and change through Antioch University — my doctoral thesis was an ethnographic study of blind adults who are successfully employed in large American corporations. So I interviewed blind people who are working at all the name brand companies that we all know. And there were nine themes that emerged around what were the conditions that allowed people to be successful and create these successful career pathways. And blindness skills was prominently featured. So people had to have blindness skills. If they were Braille readers — there was a variety. So some people were low vision and could use magnification, but everyone used technology. Everyone used some sort of technology. The blind people were all Braille readers. And orientation and mobility really came up. You have to be able to travel independently and safely through the world. If you’re going to be in the world of work, you’re going to have to navigate workplaces. Many of these folks traveled for work, so [you] need to be able to maneuver an airport and get on planes, trains and automobiles. And so I know that you at Braille Institute also realize the importance of strong orientation and mobility skills. And you have Cane Quest, and I’d like to hear a little bit about that.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So for those who don’t know, orientation is really the concept of knowing where you are and where you’re trying to go, and what pathway you should take. So being oriented to your surroundings and your destinations. And mobility is the concept around being able to move through spaces efficiently and safely and gracefully. Most people do that with either a long white cane, which is what I use — I learned to use when I was six — or a dog guide, or some combination of those things. So let’s hear a little about Cane Quest.

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely. So Cane Quest is our orientation mobility program. It’s been around since 2009. And Cane Quest is about building confidence and independence. It gives blind and low vision students the opportunity to practice and demonstrate real world orientation and mobility skills in a fun and supportive environment. It turns the skills that students practice in everyday life — like using a cane, navigating routes, crossing streets, identifying landmarks, and problem solving — into an experience they can be proud of. It makes mobility fun. And this year, in addition to last year — this is year two — that Cane Quest is taking that experience somewhere completely new: the Los Angeles Zoo. So we’re giving students a chance to use their own skills in a real dynamic environment rather than a traditional classroom or school setting. The zoo is such a fun setting, because there are sounds, smells…

Dr. Kirk Adams: That’s making me smile. That sounds like fun.

Rachel Antoine: Yes. Sounds, smells, pathways, landmarks, people, and unexpected situations that students have to navigate. It makes the experience feel like a real adventure. And students will work through different [unclear 00:35:32] navigating stations. It’s also a great community and family day, for the general public to see what young blind youth are capable of. We’re putting independence and mobility skills front and center. So it’s such a fun program that is happening. Our SoCal regional is happening October 3rd at the LA Zoo. We’re also partnering with LA Galaxy, our soccer team, and Guide Dogs of America, who are bringing ten guide dog puppies.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Nice.

Rachel Antoine: So we’re really, really excited. It reinforces that idea that blind and low vision kids should have access to the same opportunities to explore, learn, have fun, and participate in their community. So that’s what this is about.

Dr. Kirk Adams: That’s awesome. So Rachel, you are doing great work. Braille Institute, kudos to the whole team.

Rachel Antoine: Thank you so much.

Dr. Kirk Adams: It was great to be at Braille Challenge again this year. I hope to be back soon.

Rachel Antoine: Absolutely.

Dr. Kirk Adams: So I jotted down that if people want to reach out to you by email, it’s braillechallenge@brailleinstitute.org.

Rachel Antoine: Yes. So that’s our main one. Yes.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yeah. And there is a separate website, https://braillechallenge.org. People can reach out to you and learn more and get involved. For me — if you want to get in touch with me, I’m on LinkedIn every day. It’s Kirk Adams, PhD on LinkedIn. And then my website is DR as in doctor — https://drkirkadams.com. I have a newsletter you can sign up for. I have a link to my book, which came out in July. It’s called The Disability Dividend: Supercharge Your Bottom Line Through Disability Inclusion, which is geared toward employers who are out there battling to attract and retain the best and brightest talent — how to do that by being inclusive of people with disabilities. And I’d love to talk to anyone, anytime, about any way I could be helpful in creating opportunities for blind people to thrive in this world, whatever thriving means to them. Especially interested in creating pathways for blind kids to move into adulthood and flourish and thrive. So Braille is important. Essential. Good orientation mobility skills is a must. And Rachel, you’re helping make that happen. So I really appreciate you having me. Thank you to Braille Challenge. I’m glad you were here with me today. And keep up the good work. And I’m looking forward to seeing Brailled It this weekend.

Rachel Antoine: Yes, yes, yes. Thank you so much. Thank you so much for having me today. And at the heart of all of this, we just want one message: access creates opportunity, and representation shows people what’s possible. So get involved, spread the word, and help us make sure that Braille opportunity and possibility are accessible to everyone. So we’re doing that through Braille Challenge and Cane Quest. item.title: When Disclosure Costs You the Interview: Seattle’s Disability:IN Chapter Takes on the Question I Lived
item.dc:creator: Dr. Kirk Adams
item.description:
Here, Dr. Kirk Adams tells the story of the impossible choice that shaped his career. In 1983, fresh out of Whitman College with a degree in economics, he could either say nothing about his blindness and watch an interview collapse the moment he walked in with a long white cane, or disclose it at the top of his cover letter and stop getting phone interviews altogether. Two bad options, and no third one on offer. He connects that experience directly to "The Courage to Be Human at Work: Vulnerability, Access, and Connection," a free 90-minute webinar hosted by Disability:IN Washington on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, and led by Linea Johnson, Founder and CEO of The Thrive Shift. Its central question, he writes, is one he recognized on sight: how do we create workplaces where people don't have to choose between protecting themselves and belonging?

item.content:encoded:
Event Details at a Glance

  • What: The Courage to Be Human at Work: Vulnerability, Access, and Connection
  • When: Wednesday, September 30, 2026, 11:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Pacific
  • Where: Online, on Microsoft Teams
  • Cost: Free. Anyone can view and join.
  • Presenter: Linea Johnson, Founder and CEO of The Thrive Shift
  • Host: Disability:IN Washington
  • Register: https://events.teams.microsoft.com/event/b7846c1c-f48b-4bcf-8183-8358bbcc1db7@29bd5e53-6370-4fae-99be-f7620c97cbe2

In 1983, I Learned Exactly What Disclosure Costs

I graduated from Whitman College in 1983 with a degree in economics, a full academic scholarship behind me, and what I thought was a perfectly reasonable plan. I would send out a cover letter and a resume, the way everyone did, and the work would follow.

The cover letters worked. The phone interviews worked beautifully. Then I would arrive in person, with a long white cane in my hand and a slate and stylus in my bag, and I would feel the room change. The person across the desk had never worked alongside a blind colleague, and simply could not picture how I would do the job.

So I tried the other approach. I began disclosing my blindness in the cover letter, right at the top, so that nobody would have to be surprised by it.

The phone interviews stopped.

That is the whole of it. Two options, both of them bad, and no third one on offer. Disclose, and never get into the room. Say nothing, and lose the room the moment you walk into it. I was twenty-two years old and I genuinely believed the problem was me.

It was not me. It was a set of rooms that had never been designed with me in them. It took me a doctorate and an ethnographic study of eleven blind professionals to be able to say that sentence with evidence behind it, but I knew it long before I could prove it.

The Question Nobody Should Have to Answer

On Wednesday, September 30, Disability:IN Washington is hosting a free 90 minute webinar built on exactly that problem. It is called The Courage to Be Human at Work: Vulnerability, Access, and Connection, and the question at its center is one I recognize on sight:

“How do we create workplaces where people don’t have to choose between protecting themselves and belonging?”

We are all told to bring our whole selves to work. The session asks the harder follow up question, the one that actually matters to the person being advised: what does that instruction mean when being fully seen carries real risk, and when the support you need is not reliably available, understood, or safe to ask for?

What I appreciate most about how this session is framed is where it puts the burden. It does not treat vulnerability as a skill employees need to get better at. It looks instead at how workplace culture, power, accessibility and trust shape whether a person can be open at all. That is the right end of the problem to pick up.

What the Session Covers

Six threads run through the 90 minutes. Courage and vulnerability at work, and what it means to show up authentically while still holding healthy boundaries and protecting your own privacy. Masking and disclosure, including why people mask, what disclosure can open up, and the real risks that come with being open about a disability or a mental health condition. Accessibility and accommodations, and how organizations can move past treating an accommodation as an individual exception and toward workplaces simply designed for access and flexibility in the first place.

Then the practical half. Skills for employees and for managers, because this is never a one sided conversation: individuals learn to communicate what they need and advocate for themselves, and managers learn to respond to vulnerability, build trust, and create conditions where people actually have meaningful choices. Artificial intelligence and assistive technology, and how emerging tools can expand accessibility, autonomy and participation while complementing human connection rather than replacing it. And finally the human side of work, and why relationships, trust and empathy remain essential no matter how much the technology changes around us.

The last stretch is a live question and answer session, open to everyone on the call. In my experience that is where the useful part of any session like this actually happens.

Who Is Leading It

The session is led by Linea Johnson, Founder and CEO of The Thrive Shift, a consulting firm that helps organizations design more ethical, human centered workplaces and technologies by genuinely partnering with people who have lived experience. She works at the intersection of workplace mental health, disability, organizational change and responsible innovation, and she has spent more than fifteen years alongside employers, nonprofits and health organizations on workplace wellbeing and lived experience leadership.

She has advised and collaborated with One Mind, Panasonic North America and the ADA National Network, delivered the opening keynote at the National Alliance on Mental Illness national convention, and serves on One Mind’s Lived Experience Advisory Council. Her work reaches beyond the workplace too, through the World Health Organization, the award winning documentary Hidden Pictures, and her co-authored memoir Perfect Chaos, published by St. Martin’s Press and featured by NPR, Forbes and USA Today. She holds a master’s degree in healthcare leadership from Brown University and a change management certificate from Cornell.

One detail I noticed with real pleasure: Linea has served on the Washington State Governor’s Committee on Disability Issues and Employment. So have I. This state has a habit of producing people who keep turning up for this work, and that is not an accident.

Why This Particular Chapter Matters to Me

I have a long history with this organization, and it started in Seattle.

When I joined The Lighthouse for the Blind, Inc. as development director in 2000, our esteemed DeafBlind program was being led by Marthalee Galeota. She went on to build a career in accessibility and disability leadership at Starbucks, where she has led the company’s disability initiatives and its interpreter services, and where she is also a nationally certified American Sign Language interpreter with specialist skills in Braille and tactile interpreting.

Marthalee is the reason I know this organization at all. While I was serving as the Lighthouse’s general manager of administration, she urged me to go to a national meeting of the U.S. Business Leadership Network in the Washington, D.C. area. It was held at the labyrinthine Gaylord at National Harbor in Maryland, which was a considerable orientation and mobility challenge all by itself. My recollection is roughly 300 people in the room, most of them human resources specialists trying to work out how to hire a few people with disabilities.

Shortly after that trip, the Lighthouse got involved with WSBLN, the Washington Business Leadership Network. We hosted chapter meetings in our own building. That chapter is the direct ancestor of the one hosting this webinar, and the chapter says so itself: its site today reads “Disability:IN Washington, formerly WSBLN.”

So when an invitation from Disability:IN Washington landed in my inbox this month, it did not read to me like a newsletter. It read like a room I used to sit in, still going.

Where the Business Leadership Network Actually Came From

The history here is worth getting right, because it is better than most people assume.

The Business Leadership Network model was created in 1994 out of the President’s Committee on Employment of People with Disabilities, the federal body that later became the U.S. Department of Labor’s Office of Disability Employment Policy. It was built as an employer led coalition, and the national network was co-sponsored by a partnership between the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the U.S. Department of Labor. This was never a charity initiative bolted onto business. It was business, with the federal government holding the door.

The national organization that supported those local chapters, the U.S. Business Leadership Network, was incorporated in 2003. By the time I was attending, John Kemp was its executive director and general counsel, a role the Department of Labor recorded by name when it signed a formal alliance with the USBLN to promote the employment of people with disabilities. Kemp went on to lead The Viscardi Center, which is a pleasing coincidence for me personally, because in 2024 I was honored with the Henry Viscardi Achievement Award.

In 2018 the USBLN became Disability:IN. Same lineage, much larger ambition.

What Disability:IN Looks Like Today

If you have not run across the organization before, here is the short orientation. Disability:IN describes itself simply: it partners with business to globally advance disability inclusion. Go to its site and open the corporate partners page, and you will find a long list of major companies that have committed to disability inclusion in their hiring, in how they create and market products and services, and in whether disability owned business enterprises appear in their supply chains.

It runs an annual benchmark that lets companies measure their own disability inclusion practices against their peers, and it certifies Disability Owned Business Enterprises so that corporate buyers can find them. Over nearly thirty years it has grown from a handful of local employer coalitions into a genuine force. It also still runs on state chapters, which is the part that matters this month.

I Have Registered, and I Hope You Will Too

I have signed up for this one. It is free, it is online, and anyone can view and join, so there is nothing standing between you and the room.

If you care about disability employment, come. And then please forward the invitation to the other disability employment champions inside your own company and your own network, because the people who most need to hear a session on disclosure are very often the managers who have never once had to think about it.

Register here: https://events.teams.microsoft.com/event/b7846c1c-f48b-4bcf-8183-8358bbcc1db7@29bd5e53-6370-4fae-99be-f7620c97cbe2

I could not choose, in 1983, between protecting myself and belonging. Nobody handed me a third option, so I spent a decade selling municipal bonds over the telephone instead, where my blindness was nobody’s business because nobody could see me. It worked out. It should not have had to.

Building the third option is what this work is for. And it remains what I have said for most of my career: inclusion is not just the right thing to do, it is a strategic advantage.

item.title: Another Door to Knock On: Jennifer Bazer and the Palmetto Council of the Blind
item.dc:creator: Dr. Kirk Adams
item.description:
Here, Dr. Kirk Adams introduces Jennifer Bazer, President of the Palmetto Council of the Blind of South Carolina and a newly elected member of the Board of Directors of the American Council of the Blind, and makes the case for supporting the Council's Kicking for a Cause online auction, which closes on September 20, 2026. Blind since birth, a social worker by training and a veteran of more than a decade managing large federal workforce programs, Bazer founded the Palmetto Council in 2023 with a deliberately simple aim: to give a newly blind South Carolinian, a family member who does not know where to turn, or anyone looking for a way in "another door they could knock on."

item.content:encoded:
People ask me to help spread the word about things almost every week. I say yes often, and I say no more often than I would like to. Every so often, though, something reaches me that I would have gone looking for had it not found me first. This is one of those.

The Palmetto Council of the Blind of South Carolina is running an online auction called Kicking for a Cause. It is open now and it closes on September 20, 2026. There are 35 items on the board, bids start as low as ten dollars, and every dollar raised goes to work in South Carolina. You can find it here: https://scblind.betterworld.org/auctions/kicking-cause

That is the practical information, and if it is all you take from this article, it is enough. But it is not why I am writing. I am writing because of a sentence.

The Sentence

Jennifer Bazer, who serves as President of the Palmetto Council of the Blind, wrote to me about why the organization exists. This is what she said:

“I wanted someone who was newly losing their sight, a family member who didn’t know where to turn, a blind person looking for resources, or someone wanting to become more involved to have another door they could knock on in South Carolina.”

Another door to knock on. I have been blind since I was five years old, when my retinas detached, and I have spent more than thirty years working in and around the blindness field. I have run two national organizations. I have testified, consulted, fundraised, and sat on more boards than I can comfortably list. And I am not sure I have read a better six-word description of what a community organization is actually for.

Not a mission statement. Not a strategic plan. A door. Somewhere to go when you do not yet know what you need.

Who Jennifer Bazer Is

Jennifer has been blind since birth. She is President of the Palmetto Council of the Blind and was recently elected to the Board of Directors of the American Council of the Blind. She is a social worker by education, and she spent more than ten years in workforce development, most recently leading teams and managing large federal workforce programs and contracts.

I want to pause on that last part, because it matters and it is the sort of thing that gets skipped over in a fundraising appeal. Managing large federal workforce programs is not adjacent work. It is hard, unglamorous, deeply operational work, and the people who do it well understand exactly how opportunity gets built and exactly where it leaks away. Jennifer did that for a living, and then she chose to build something in her own state.

She is also, in her own words, a mother of two teenagers:

“So when I talk about independence, opportunity, expectations, leadership and community, those aren’t simply professional concepts to me. They have been woven throughout my life.”

What South Carolina Was Missing

The Palmetto Council of the Blind was founded in 2023. That makes it young, and Jennifer is direct about what she was determined it would not become:

“I didn’t want another organization that simply existed on paper or held a meeting once a month. I wanted us to build relationships.”

Anyone who has worked in the nonprofit world knows how many organizations do exist mostly on paper, and knows that it is rarely anyone’s fault. Volunteers burn out. Founders move. The meeting becomes the mission. Deciding at the outset that you are going to be a real presence in people’s lives is a much heavier commitment than it sounds, and it is the commitment Jennifer made.

She describes what people actually arrive needing as a kind of ladder, and I think it is worth reading exactly as she wrote it.

“Sometimes what someone needs is very practical: a white cane, locator dots, a magnifier, accessible information or help finding a resource.”

“Sometimes what they need is a connection.”

“Sometimes it is the opportunity to attend a convention, meet other blind people, hear what they are doing, discover technology or resources they didn’t know existed, and come home thinking a little differently about what might be possible in their own life.”

“And sometimes they simply need someone to answer the phone or an email and say, ‘Let’s figure this out.’”

I have been in that third sentence. I have watched a person walk into a convention hall carrying the assumption that their life had just narrowed permanently, and walk out three days later having quietly revised it. Nothing was fixed. Nobody’s vision came back. What changed was the evidence available to them about what a blind person’s life can contain, and that evidence came from being in a room with people living it.

That is not a soft outcome. It is one of the most durable interventions I know of, and it costs the price of getting somebody to a convention.

A Community That Expects Something from You

Here is the line in Jennifer’s letter that stopped me, and the reason I wanted to write this rather than simply forward a link.

“My own experiences have shown me how much it matters for people who are blind to have access not only to tools and resources, but to information, opportunities, relationships and a community that expects something from them.”

A community that expects something from them.

I attended the Oregon State School for the Blind as a boy, and when I am asked what it gave me I always name three things: blindness skills, a sense of agency, and high expectations. The third one is the one people are least prepared for. We are comfortable talking about tools and training. We are far less comfortable saying out loud that a blind child should be expected to produce, to contribute, and to be held to a standard.

When I wrote my doctoral dissertation, I interviewed blind adults who were successfully employed at large American corporations and asked them what had produced that success. Nine factors emerged from those conversations. One of the strongest was expectation, the expectation of family, of teachers, of the people around them. Not encouragement. Not support. Expectation, which is a different and more demanding thing.

So when a blind woman in South Carolina tells me she is building an organization designed to expect something of the people it serves, she is not describing a nice-to-have. She is describing the exact mechanism my own research found decisive, delivered at the level of a state where somebody can actually reach it.

That is why I am asking you to bid.

What Is Actually in the Auction

I looked at the auction board myself before writing this, because I do not like recommending things I have not examined. There are 35 items, and the range is wider than I expected.

If you want to participate for the price of a sandwich, you can. Bidding opens at ten dollars on several items, including a Westbrook Brewing gift card, a DoorDash gift card, a Wingard’s Market certificate, a bath and body care set, and two novels by Daisy Russell. Fifteen dollars opens the bidding on Tidal Wave Auto Spa car wash passes, a set of titanium cutting boards, and a signed softcover and eBook of Words of Life by Ann Chiappetta.

In the middle of the board there are gift cards to Starbucks, Walmart, Target and Hamburger Joe’s, a 75 dollar Mountain Mist certificate, a Columbia Fireflies fan experience package, two dōTERRA essential oils wellness collections, a REVIVE essential oils starter kit, an Oh Clementine luxe gold jewelry set, a custom watercolor pet portrait by Amanda House, a sparrow note card collection by Laura Senn Day, a pound of gourmet chocolate fudge, and four hand-poured premium candles that at the time I looked were the most fiercely contested item on the board.

There is an autographed Dawn Staley basketball, which I suspect will not stay quiet for long.

And there are four travel and experience packages for anyone in a position to go big: Discover Amazing Asheville, a personal cooking lesson from a top chef, Unforgettable Glamping Near the Mountains, and Country Music in Music City.

Two items in particular tell you what kind of organization this is. One is a 100 dollar Ambutech electronic gift certificate. The other is called, simply, the Low Vision Entertainment and Independence Basket.

Those sit on the same board as a basketball and a getaway to Asheville, and that is exactly right. The people Palmetto serves are not a category. They are South Carolinians who need a magnifier and also want to go to a ball game.

There is also a year-round shop with no bidding at all, where a fixed price gets you a Palmetto Council T-shirt, a Blind Pirate Soap Company gift set, or a camping stay at Shenandoah Crossing Resort: https://scblind.betterworld.org/campaigns/palmetto-council-shop

I will also name the businesses that donated, because they did not have to and because the disability community notices who shows up: Ambutech, BarkBox, Blind Pirate Soap, dōTERRA Essential Oils, Hamburger Joe’s, Mountain Mist, Oh Clementine, REVIVE Essential Oils, Tidal Wave Auto Spa, Westbrook Brewing Company, and Wingard’s Market.

What Your Bid Actually Buys

This is where a lot of fundraising appeals go vague. Jennifer’s does not. Here is where the money goes, in her words:

“Funds raised help us provide white canes, locator dots, magnifiers, accessible materials and other resources; offer assistance to members; support education and outreach throughout South Carolina; and provide opportunities for members to participate in state and national conventions.”

White canes. Locator dots. Magnifiers. These are not expensive items, and that is the point. A white cane is one of the highest-return purchases in the whole field: it is inexpensive, it lasts, and it is the difference between a person who can leave the house alone and a person who cannot. A ten dollar bid on a gift card is not a symbolic gesture in that economy. It is a real contribution to a real object that goes to a real person.

And then there are the conventions, which brings us back to the third rung of Jennifer’s ladder. Somebody goes, meets other blind people, finds out that technology exists that they had never heard of, and, in her phrase, comes home thinking a little differently about what might be possible in their own life. I have watched that happen more times than I can count. It is the closest thing to a reliable lever that I know.

Jennifer frames the whole thing in a way I want to underline, because it is the correct frame:

“It is not fundraising simply for the sake of raising money. Every bid helps give a relatively young organization the ability to reach farther, provide more resources, create more opportunities and be there when someone in South Carolina reaches out.”

That is capacity, not charity. You are not relieving suffering with a bid on a car wash package. You are extending the reach of an organization that answers the phone.

Four Ways to Help, Closing September 20

Jennifer offers four, and I am passing all four along because not everyone can do the first one and the fourth one genuinely matters.

  • Bid. 35 items, bidding closes September 20, 2026: https://scblind.betterworld.org/auctions/kicking-cause
  • Shop. Open year-round, fixed prices, no bidding required: https://scblind.betterworld.org/campaigns/palmetto-council-shop
  • Donate. If bidding is not for you, give directly at https://scblind.org
  • Share. In Jennifer’s words, even if someone is not able to contribute financially, sharing the auction and shop with others is a wonderful way to help. Forward this. Post it. Send it to one person in South Carolina.

Questions, or an item you would like to donate, go to info@scblind.org 📧️

Back to the Door

Somewhere in South Carolina this month, a person is going to be told by a doctor that their vision is not coming back. Somewhere in South Carolina this month, a daughter is going to start searching for what to do about her father, and she is going to find very little.

Whether there is a door for those two people to knock on is not a matter of fate. It is a matter of whether a small organization founded in 2023 has the resources to keep the lights on and somebody available to answer.

The auction closes September 20, 2026. Jennifer put it more simply than I can:

“People can bid, shop, donate or simply share our story. All of those things help.”

Go get in the game: https://scblind.betterworld.org/auctions/kicking-cause

item.description:
Here, Dr. Kirk Adams reflects on launching the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion on September 1, in a span of days that also brought the deaths of Dolly Parton, Wendell Berry, and Gloria Steinem. He writes candidly about his discomfort at honoring three white figures in a piece about a coalition devoted to diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and belonging, and he insists that the long struggle for freedom has been led, sustained, and repeatedly rescued by Black people, Indigenous people, people of color, women, LGBTQ+ people, people with disabilities, immigrants, workers, and countless others whose names never reach a history book. What he draws from each of the three is a lesson in using one's gifts in service to others: Parton's Imagination Library, whose Braille Tales partnership with the American Printing House for the Blind fills his own bookshelf with print-and-braille titles his two-year-old granddaughter brings him with the words "Grandpa, read book with your hands!"; Berry's insistence that community is a daily practice rather than an abstract idea, the conviction behind Adams's own philosophy of brightening the corner where you are; and Steinem's advice to young women to listen to themselves rather than to her, together with her understanding that movements require infrastructure and not merely admired personalities.

item.content:encoded:
On September 1, we launched the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion.

The launch came one week after the death of Dolly Parton and one day after the death of Wendell Berry. Then, two days later came the news that Gloria Steinem had died.

Three remarkable lives. Three profoundly different voices. Three people who, each in their own way, helped bend the arc of the moral universe toward justice.

And now they are gone.

I confess that I feel some tension writing about three white people in connection with a Coalition devoted to expanding diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and belonging.

We must never tell the history of social justice as though progress has been bestowed upon us by a handful of famous white people. The long struggle for freedom has been led, sustained, and repeatedly rescued by Black people, Indigenous people, people of color, women, LGBTQ+ people, people with disabilities, immigrants, workers, and countless others whose names may never appear in a history book.

Dolly Parton, Wendell Berry, and Gloria Steinem were not perfect. None of us is. Nor were they the sole authors of the movements with which they became associated.

But each demonstrated something important about how people can use their gifts, influence, resources, and voices in service to others.

Dolly Parton: Building Belonging Through Books, Music, and Love

Recently, my wife, Ros, was listening to Brittany Packnett Cunningham’s podcast in our kitchen. I overheard Brittany say something to the effect of:

“I’m going to have to have a talk with the Grim Reaper. You are taking the wrong people. You are taking the wrong white people!”

This was after Dolly Parton’s death but before we lost Wendell Berry and Gloria Steinem.

Brittany went on to reflect on how Dolly made music for everyone and consistently supported people of color and LGBTQ+ people.

Dolly possessed the rare ability to reach across many of the boundaries that divide us. Her music welcomed people in. Her warmth made people feel that they belonged. She publicly supported LGBTQ+ rights, affirmed the Black Lives Matter movement, invested in a predominantly Black Nashville neighborhood, and used her visibility to make room for people whom much of the country music establishment had overlooked or excluded.

Her most transformative legacy, however, may be found in the hands of children.

Created in honor of her father, who could not read, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has given hundreds of millions of books to young children. Dolly once said:

“If I’m remembered 100 years from now, I hope it will be not for looks but for books.”

I understand the power of that legacy in a deeply personal way.

On my bookshelf are several dozen children’s books containing both print and braille. They came through Braille Tales, a partnership between the American Printing House for the Blind and Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. The program enables blind and low-vision children, and sighted children and their blind grownups, to share accessible books as families.

My four-year-old grandson and two-year-old granddaughter know that when they want Grandpa to read them a story, they must bring me a book with braille in it.

Recently, my granddaughter brought one of those books to me and said:

“Grandpa, read book with your hands!”

That is Dolly Parton’s legacy in my home.

A little girl understands that her blind grandfather reads differently, and that different is perfectly natural. She does not see an obstacle. She sees another way to share a story.

That is inclusion.

That is belonging.

That is love made practical.

The American Printing House for the Blind continues to make this family experience possible through Braille Tales.

Wendell Berry: Caring for the Corner Where We Stand

Wendell Berry influenced me in another way.

As a writer, poet, farmer, environmentalist, and cultural critic, he reminded us that community is not an abstract idea. It is a daily practice rooted in how we treat the people, creatures, land, and institutions closest to us.

Berry wrote:

“The community, in the fullest sense: a place and all its creatures, is the smallest unit of health.”

That conviction has long shaped my own philosophy: brighten the corner where you are.

We can and must confront national systems of injustice. But we must also examine what is happening in our workplaces, schools, neighborhoods, congregations, families, and community organizations.

Who is being heard?

Who is being overlooked?

Who is welcomed through the front door but excluded from real influence?

Who has knowledge and talent but no pathway to leadership?

Berry taught that we do not heal in isolation. We heal through relationships, responsibility, reciprocity, and care for place.

His life asks us a stubborn and necessary question: What are we doing with the particular corner entrusted to us?

Gloria Steinem: Opening Doors and Listening to Women

As a husband, father, brother, colleague, and friend, I am profoundly grateful for Gloria Steinem’s work to advance the freedom, dignity, safety, and leadership of women.

Steinem helped expose discrimination that society had normalized. She co-founded Ms. magazine, the National Women’s Political Caucus, and other organizations that changed public conversation and expanded women’s political and cultural power.

Importantly, she also understood that leadership is not about asking younger people to imitate those who came before them.

When asked what advice she would give young women, she said:

“Listen to yourselves, not to me.”

What a remarkable instruction for an elder and a leader to offer.

Do not become a copy of me.

Do not wait for my permission.

Listen to your experience. Trust your voice. Organize around the realities of your generation.

Steinem described herself as an “entrepreneur of social change.” She understood that movements require more than admired personalities. They require organizations, networks, stories, resources, relationships, and pathways through which people can exercise power together.

That is precisely the kind of infrastructure we must build now.

Inheritance Is Not Enough

We can honor these three lives without placing them at the center of every struggle or overlooking the generations of diverse leaders who fought beside them, challenged them, taught them, and made broader movements possible.

Honoring our elders does not mean placing them on pedestals.

It means carrying the work forward.

We are living through a generational transition. Many leaders who shaped the struggles of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries are leaving us. Their deaths create grief, but they also create a responsibility.

Who will step forward?

Who will mentor them?

Who will fund their ideas?

Who will give them room to lead. Not someday, after waiting patiently for a seat at the table, but now?

Too many organizations say they want younger and more diverse leaders while continuing to concentrate authority, visibility, relationships, and resources in the same hands.

We cannot develop the next generation merely by inviting young people into the room. We must share power, provide meaningful opportunities, listen to their analysis, invest in their growth, and remain open to being challenged by them.

Mentorship must also be mutual.

Established leaders have experience, history, relationships, and hard-earned lessons to share. Emerging leaders bring new language, new tools, new cultural understanding, new forms of organizing, and questions that institutions desperately need to hear.

The goal is not to pass an old torch unchanged.

The goal is to build a larger fire together.

This Is Why the Coalition Exists

The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion is committed to working with, mentoring, supporting, and learning from the next generation of social justice champions.

We want to connect people across race, disability, gender, generation, affectional orientation, culture, profession, geography, identity, and lived experience.

We want experienced leaders, emerging leaders, reluctant leaders, and people who have never imagined themselves as leaders.

We need elders who are willing to share what they know without controlling what comes next.

We need younger people willing to question our assumptions, stretch our imaginations, and create approaches we have not yet considered.

We need people from historically excluded communities to exercise real influence, not serve as decorations in someone else’s vision of diversity.

The Coalition is a place to exchange resources, develop new ideas, mentor and be mentored, organize, advocate, build relationships, and transform isolated individual effort into collective power.

Connect. Learn. Act. Together.

Every generation inherits unfinished work.

Our responsibility is to honor what came before us, repair what was broken, preserve what remains valuable, and create smoother pathways for those coming next.

Become a Founding Member

We are building this Coalition right now, and we need you.

Do not stand on the sidelines and wait for someone else to protect inclusion, equal opportunity, belonging, social justice, human rights, and human dignity.

Bring your experience.

Bring your questions.

Bring your relationships.

Bring your imagination.

And bring someone from another generation with you.

Dolly Parton showed us that a book placed in a child’s hands can open a world.

Wendell Berry showed us that healthy lives require healthy communities.

Gloria Steinem showed us that movements grow when people listen to their own voices and to one another.

Now the work belongs to us.

Let us honor those who came before by opening doors for those who are coming next.

Let us resist fear, division, isolation, and hate.

Access Awareness: Updates That Matter ♿️

Support Our Fight for Inclusion & Human Dignity for All

Here, Dr. Kirk Adams and the Institute for Sustainable Diversity & Inclusion make the case for the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion in the plainest terms they have used yet. We are living through an orchestrated assault on diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and belonging, the campaign argues, and the retreat is neither inevitable nor permanent. Programs are being dismantled, leaders isolated or pushed out, civil rights organizations targeted and intimidated, and the people doing the work, often the same people most directly harmed when it disappears, are carrying the emotional, professional, and financial weight of this moment largely alone. The Coalition is the structural answer to that isolation: a national online home built on the Circle platform under the umbrella of ISDI, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, where practitioners, affected community members, allies, educators, and changemakers can convene, trade resources and expertise, support one another, and organize together instead of weathering this separately. The campaign refuses to describe that as a nice idea. It calls it infrastructure, alignment, and power, built intentionally.

The ask is specific, and the progress behind it is real. Standing the platform up, setup, implementation, onboarding, and the first year of use, costs roughly $20,000, and since the fundraiser opened on June 22, 2026 it has raised $8,758 from 58 donors, about 44 percent of the way there. Gifts are tax deductible and every level is spelled out plainly: $25 widens outreach, $50 supports programming and member engagement, $100 funds platform tools and implementation, $250 underwrites workshops and peer learning, and $500 or more builds the infrastructure a sustainable national coalition actually needs. The appeal is signed by Kirk Adams, Barbara Deane, Effenus Henderson, Joseph Marth, Amelia Ransom, Eddie Pate, Constance Durham-Engelstad, and Jacob Davidson, and it closes on the sentence that gives the whole effort its shape: your gift is not simply helping fund a platform, it is helping build a community of resistance, resilience, strategy, and hope at a time when all four are urgently needed. Give, or send it to someone who should.

This Month’s Featured Advertisement ️

Help Shape the Future of Healthcare: Join Rare Patient Voice Through Dr. Kirk Adams

If you’re a patient or caregiver who wants to make a difference, I invite you to join Rare Patient Voice through my personal referral link: https://rarepatientvoice.com/rp/DrKirk.

Rare Patient Voice connects individuals living with rare and non-rare conditions to paid research opportunities where your voice directly shapes new treatments, products, and policies. Participants are typically compensated $120 per hour for surveys, interviews, and focus groups. It’s a powerful way to ensure your lived experience helps improve care for others, and you’ll be compensated for your time.

By signing up through my link, you’re also supporting our shared mission of making healthcare more inclusive and patient-driven.
