News 📰️

1.) The Doors Are Open: How to Join the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion | Dr. Kirk Adams, Executive Director, ISDI | September 7, 2026

Here, Dr. Kirk Adams announces that the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion went live on September 1, 2026, opened not with a webinar or a panel but with an “Ask Us Anything” hour of questions, frustrations, ideas and lived experience. He explains what the Coalition actually is: a way for members to move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power, built on four words, Connect, Learn, Act, Together. He is direct about who it is for, which is everybody, and equally direct that disability inclusion and accessibility are not a side room in it but a dedicated space by design. Inside, he describes three things above all others: BELONG, the peer circles where saying “I am overwhelmed” is met with practical help rather than judgment; CLARITY, a trusted translation layer of plain-language briefings and expert-guided sessions; and POWER, the shared tools, cross-sector strategy and coalition-backed influence that turn isolated effort into coordinated action. In practice that means Ask the Experts office hours, a Member Lounge and Directory, a growing Resource Library, a Rapid Response Hub for the moments that will not wait, legislative and legal updates, podcasts featuring DEIAB voices, and a shared calendar of events worth your time.

2.) Recording: Official Launch of The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion | Dr. Kirk Adams, Executive Director, ISDI | September 7, 2026

Here, Dr. Kirk Adams shares the full recording of the September 1, 2026 public launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, the national membership community created by the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion to help people working in diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and belonging move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power.

3.) Braille Is Beautiful, and Braille Is Literacy | DrKirkAdams.com | August 25, 2026

Braille literacy remains essential alongside screen readers, Aaron Di Blasi writes, arguing that tactile reading preserves direct access to spelling, punctuation, formatting, mathematics, and private note-taking. He also challenges the widely repeated claim that only 10% of blind people read braille: a 2022 systematic review found no current nationally representative U.S. measure.

4.) Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams: Interview With Tom Babinszki, Owner, Even Grounds | DrKirkAdams.com | August 20, 2026

Tom Babinszki, owner of Even Grounds, describes building tactile 3D models and accessibility plans for cultural venues after decades in digital accessibility, including teaching thousands at IBM. Projects include tactile work for the Toledo Zoo, Detroit Symphony Orchestra and Cincinnati Opera, plus a Braille map reproduction and restroom-layout maps.

5.) Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams: Interview With Cazerny Bussey, Founder, Even Though I’m Blind Foundation | DrKirkAdams.com | August 18, 2026

Cazerny Bussey recounts losing his sight at 15 and building the Even Though I’m Blind Foundation to expand visibility for blind creators and entrepreneurs. The foundation operates a radio station featuring roughly 45 independent blind artists, a community storytelling podcast, and a curated directory of blind-owned businesses.

6.) Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams: Interview With Jeremy Grandstaff, Executive Director, the Inspiration Foundation | DrKirkAdams.com | August 11, 2026

Jeremy Grandstaff, six months into his role as executive director of the Inspiration Foundation, outlines a two-sided disability-employment strategy: grants for training organizations and an Inspiration Seal program for employers. The foundation aims to raise the disability employment rate by 10% in five years and is redesigning Dining in the Dark events around education and executive roundtables.

7.) Podcasts by Dr. Kirk Adams: Interview With Mindy Kolin, Director of Development & Industry Partnerships at Teach Access, and Kate Sonka, Executive Director | DrKirkAdams.com | August 6, 2026

Teach Access says it reached more than 1.5 million students in 2025, surpassing its 2020 goal of 1 million by 2030 five years early. Executive Director Kate Sonka and Mindy Kolin describe the nonprofit’s faculty-first strategy: training educators to add accessibility to existing courses, supported by a fellowship, Summer Institute and open curriculum repository.

item.description:
Here, Dr. Kirk Adams shares the full recording of the September 1, 2026 public launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, the national membership community created by the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion to help people working in diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and belonging move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power.

item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, September 1, 2026, the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion publicly launched the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion. The full recording of that hour is below, along with a complete transcript of everything that was said.

The Coalition is a national, member-driven community created to help people working in diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and belonging move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power. It is a program of ISDI, built on the Circle platform, with companion apps for iOS and Android.

Board President Dr. Joseph Marth opened the event by naming the moment plainly: a sustained, aggressive and pervasive assault on diversity, equity and inclusion, and the case for a coalition as a counterforce built on courage, collaboration and collective action. ISDI’s co-directors, board members and community advisors then each spoke to why this work is personal to them. Jacob Davidson walked through the Coalition’s new home space by space, and the hour closed with an open forum on accessibility, on privacy for members whose jobs are at risk, and on how to tell this story more effectively.

Founding membership is open through December 31, 2026. Founding members are invited to help shape the membership tiers, the codes of conduct, the governance and the communities of practice, which is why ISDI describes the offer as co-authorship rather than early access. You can read more and join at https://community.i4sdi.org/coalition-founder.

Watch the Launch

On YouTube at: https://youtu.be/dEhcg3Y2uEg

About This Transcript

The complete transcript of the launch appears below so the event is readable at your own pace, with a screen reader or a refreshable Braille display, and searchable by anyone who would rather read than watch. It has been edited to clean verbatim: filler words, stutters and false starts are removed, while every speaker’s wording, grammar, dialect and meaning are preserved exactly as spoken. Square brackets mark an editor’s insertion or a passage where the audio was unclear, with a timestamp where one is available.

Full Transcript

Barbara Deane: Well, what do you say? Should we get started?

Joseph Marth: So, yeah, I think we should.

Barbara Deane: We’re at 20. We’re at 22.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Our board president, Joseph Marth.

Joseph Marth: Well, welcome everybody. Good morning. Good afternoon. Depending on where you’re at. Thank you for joining our historic event, which is the launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion. Woo hoo! It’s been a journey, as I say, most of the people on this call will know what I’m talking about. By way of just an overview about the coalition and kind of how this all came about, I think we can all recognize in the past few years there’s been a full-out assault on diversity, equity and inclusion. And that assault has been both aggressive and pervasive. And it’s had really adverse effects on individuals, families, communities, schools, colleges, universities, businesses, not-for-profits, you name it. It’s been a broad assault. It’s, as we said, it’s institutional, government and corporate in the attack. And we believe now is the time for DEI professionals to come together and form a coalition in order to have essentially what we’re talking is a counterforce, for us to go on the offensive to combat these destructive forces that we’re encountering. So this coalition is a national community, and people and organizations will stand together to advance sustainable diversity and inclusion with, what we say, courage, collaboration, and collective action. And so I say welcome to our launch. This is exciting. Joe, what I’d like to

Barbara Deane: I’m going to jump in just a minute. Are we recording this session?

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yes, we are.

Barbara Deane: Recording on.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Yes.

Barbara Deane: Okay. And then also I just noted that somebody has [Read.ai? 00:02:15] notes in, and it may be you, but I think that that should be taken out. I don’t know whose they are.

Mai Ling Chan: It was, but if you would like, we can have that removed.

Effenus Henderson: Yeah. I don’t think that, Barbara, I’m sort of in your account as opposed to mine. I don’t know why.

Terry Loving: What’s happening? Maybe me. Let me look to see how to cancel it.

Jeremy Grandstaff: It was me as well. That’s how I know what I did.

Dr. Kirk Adams: I think [Quelonna? 00:02:51]. [Quelonna?]’s in charge. She can kick those robots out.

Barbara Deane: Yeah. Take it out. Take it out.

Dr. Kirk Adams: I’ll take out the robots.

Barbara Deane: Thank you.

Mai Ling Chan: Yeah. Of course.

Dr. Kirk Adams: Well.

Barbara Deane: All right. I’m sorry, Joe. Sorry to interrupt.

Joseph Marth: That’s all right, Barbara. Let’s see. I’m going to ask each of the ISDI leaders, staff members, community advisors, board members to introduce themselves, and ask that each of them speak from the heart as to why DEI is personally and professionally meaningful to them, and why the coalition is very important. I’ll start out and I’ll just say that the coalition’s work is deeply personal to me, both professionally and personally. Professionally, as an industrial organizational psychologist, I’ve been involved in DEI work since the early 90s. Now I’ve dated myself. There you go. Thankfully, I was just a teenager when I was doing that work. A child genius. As to why this is personally important to me as a member of the LGBTQ plus community, I can’t even talk today. It’s not a concept that is just something I’ve studied or taught or helped organizations with putting into or implementing DEI. But on a personal level, I know what it’s like, that things like fighting for acceptance and equal opportunity and the freedom to be who you are is something that we have to fight for in order to attain it and to retain it. And so I feel like I’ve been bullied on the schoolyard. And I don’t like it. And I’m happy to say I’ve got some good friends on the schoolyard that feeling the same way and we’re ready to kind of say it ends now. So with that I’ll turn it over to Barbara, who not only can talk about those two things, but a little bit about ISDI as well, if you would. Barbara.

Barbara Deane: Hi everyone. My name is Barbara Deane and I am the co-director of ISDI, and I’m also the co-founder of the Northwest Diversity Learning Series. And so I just wanted to give you a little history. All this work started back in 1988 when my husband, Doctor Carlos Gil, who was a professor at the university, and I decided to start a newsletter, and the topic became cultural diversity at work. And so we published for ten years. And then in 1998, I met Susan Funk from New York, who had moved to Seattle. And we got the harebrained idea that we should start some kind of an educational forum in Seattle. And so in 1998, we started the Northwest Diversity Learning Series, and that was 28 years ago. And so the series has been running nonstop for 28 years in the Seattle area. And of course, with the pandemic, we had to go online. So now everything is online, even though everybody misses the in-person sessions that we used to hold at Nordstrom, nobody really wants to go back to that when you get right down to it.

Barbara Deane: So we’re still virtual. And then so I ran the series for ten years, and then I retired, and I retired until about 2015. And I’ll tell you what happened then. Diversity, equity and inclusion has been very important to me. It was important to me back in 1988 when I realized that there were all kinds of issues in the workplace. I got called in to one of them, a racial incident at the University of Washington Dental School, and I thought, good heavens, there must be people all over this country who wonder how to deal with these kinds of things. And are we doing the best that we can do? And that was the genesis of the newsletter that we began publishing. I think I really got my start on diversity with my family, because my family were moved into Ohio from New England and they talked funny and they had different ideas about how things were to be done. So I kind of got introduced to cross-cultural living as a child. Anyway, that’s who I am. It’s all yours.

Effenus Henderson: Thanks, Barbara. And Barbara and I started the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion back in 2015. And it was something that we wanted to continue. Barbara talked about how she had launched it and retired, and several firms, including [Archbright? 00:07:54], picked up the series for a while, and in 2015 we decided to come together. Barbara had asked me, would you take it over? And I had just retired. I come out of private industry, working for Weyerhaeuser Company for 40 years in a variety of roles, including that of chief diversity officer. And so we put our heads together and started developing the series. And it was in person down at Nordstrom for a number of years. And we found that a very good opportunity to bring in thought leaders on emerging DEI topics from around the country. And it added in terms of people’s ability to fellowship, to connect, to collaborate and share ideas about pressing issues that we’re facing in their organizations and so forth. And so over the years, we developed that. I think I’ll speak later about how we came to form the coalition. It actually started a little bit more than a year ago.

Effenus Henderson: And prior to that, Barbara and I and [Hayden Prince? 00:09:06] worked on building a toolkit for fortifying DEI during those early years when there’s substantial challenge, but we felt that we couldn’t do it alone. And we brainstormed and talked about, let’s see if we can put together a coalition. And so a little bit more than a year ago, we formed a coalition, we brought people together to talk about how a coalition could take it to another level. And Doctor Adams, the current [Executive Director], will tell you more about some of that. And Jacob and others that have been involved in terms of how it has evolved since that time. It’s been a wonderful opportunity. And I think more than ever now, a coalition where we, and with AI and technology amplifying and spreading information very fast, it can’t be done by one individual, one organization. It’s got to be a collaborative effort for all of us. And so that’s why we are very excited about this opportunity, and the work that the coalition will do under this Circle platform. So I’ll just stop there in the interest of time. And we’ll go from there.

Joseph Marth: Thank you. Kirk, do you want to go next, or one of the

Dr. Kirk Adams: Sure. So this is Kirk Adams. I am honored to serve as the executive director of the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, which is the host and coalition. I’m the immediate past president and CEO of the American Foundation for the Blind, Helen Keller’s organization. And I wanted to speak for a moment about Wendell Berry. He passed away yesterday, and he was a great inspiration for me and a great source of philosophical framework, communitarianism, his philosophy. He was born in August 5th, 1935 in Henry County, Kentucky, and he died in Kentucky yesterday at age 92. He was a poet, novelist. He was a farmer, environmental advocate, and he was a lifelong champion of healthy, interdependent communities, which is what we’re building here. And I just wanted to share a quote from his essay. “Health Is Membership” is the name of the essay. And he wrote, “I believe that the community, in the fullest sense, a place and all its creatures, is the smallest unit of health.” And that means to me that none of us can flourish in isolation, and that genuine inclusion calls upon us to create communities where everybody belongs and everybody’s wellbeing matters. And that’s what we’re endeavoring to do here today. So welcome to everybody.

Joseph Marth: Great. Well, thank you. Constance, do you want to jump in there?

Barbara Deane: Sure. Okay.

Constance Durham-Engelstad: Thanks, Joe. So one thing I picked up on, at least four of us, including me, have come out of retirement to do this work. You know, that’s amazing, right? We’re supposed to be drinking a margarita and being on a beach somewhere, but instead, we’re choosing to do this work because it’s so essential. So anyway, I’ve worked with Kirk for decades, and he’s the one that got me involved with ISDI. And my background is human resources organizational development, and regarding DEIAB, it is all around disability employment. And so I came on as a community advisor first, doing strategic planning for ISDI in a small role, ended up joining the board because of the coalition work. This is just so exciting and so rewarding. And what I want to do is just share a real short personal story. The coalition has already changed me as a person. It’s been very impactful. And what it’s changed for me, I’ve got a cold, so excuse me, it’s changed my everyday conversations. I’m intentionally finding more moments to connect with people of all ages and backgrounds and to talk about equal rights. And I did this recently with my granddaughter, who’s seven. She told me she met two of her favorite basketball players, Caitlin and Sophie. And I said, I wish I could have gone to a WNBA game as a kid. She asked me why I didn’t, and I said because there was not a WNBA at the time.

Constance Durham-Engelstad: And she just said, wait, what? And was so puzzled. She can’t imagine a world without the WNBA. So for effect, I also added, and girls weren’t allowed to wear pants to school back then, and that just sent her over the edge. And it was that moment that opened up our conversation about generational change. And then she learned that her great-great-grandmother couldn’t vote, that her great-grandmother could vote but was told who to vote for. But she didn’t listen and did. [At] 18 I voted and I chose for myself. So thanks to those decades of all that hard-won progress, Jordy’s generation has newer opportunities. But that does not mean the work is done. And prior to joining the coalition, I guarantee you Jordy and I would have talked more about her high-fiving Sophie than their equal rights. And this coalition is all about all of us finding new spaces and ways to connect, learn and act and work together. And it’s across all generations and communities to ensure equality for all. And that’s why I’m so excited about it. Already I’ve had so many conversations with different people that I know I would not have had, even some as recent as this month, just working on the coalition with different people. So very pleased to be here. And then of course, go Storm.

Joseph Marth: Thank you, Constance. All right. I know we have a couple other board members, Amelia and Doctor Eddie Pate. Amelia Ransom, I don’t know if you’re available and can do an intro. We’d love to hear from you.

Amelia Ransom: It’s probably a little loud where I am, so I’ll be brief. Constance, I also, I’m a season ticket holder to the Storm. So I want to take Caitlin Clark and Sophie from your granddaughter, and in return give her A’ja Wilson and maybe Nneka Ogwumike as her heroes, because in this coalition, we need people who support players who support all of us. So there are players who do that. Sadly, Caitlin and Sophie are not two of them. I hear you. I am here because I believe you cannot be part of a movement and not actually move. I think I owe something to the ancestors of mine who jumped from the ships, who endured what they endured over hundreds of years. I think I owe something back to them, and I think it can’t be silenced. If I believe that we hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their creator with certain unalienable rights, that among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, then I have to believe that for all people, and I have to do the work to ensure it. I think of myself as running a relay race. I don’t have to do all the work. I don’t have to run the whole race. But I have to run my leg really, really well so that eventually we win, and that I hand my baton to someone else who’s going to Sha’Carri Richardson that thing all the way to the finish line. So that is what brings me here today. I am also retired like many of the other people here. I retired, but I host a podcast called DEI AF. If you need to know what the A F stands for, DM me and I’ll be happy to let you know. But I started that because I believed I would not let DEI die on my watch, and we would continue to have the conversations and to continue to include the people who needed to be included and share information that we don’t always have access to. So that’s what brings me here today. Eddie, I’ll turn it over to you.

Eddie Pate: Thank you. And Barbara, thank you for allowing me to follow Constance and Amelia. Telling you, Eddie Pate. I’ve been involved with ISDI for a long time as a customer, when I was leading diversity efforts for the enterprise and partner group back at Microsoft back in the early 2000, all the way through to when I retired from corporate at 2018. And then eventually joined the board of ISDI. Join in Three Steps

If you already know you want in, here’s the whole thing, right up front.

  1. Go to https://community.i4sdi.org/coalition-founder and become a Founding Member.
  2. Choose monthly or annual, or the honor-system rate if that is right for you.
  3. Download the DEIAB Community Coalition app for iPhone and iPad, or the same app on Google Play. It works just as well in a browser.

Founding Membership is $25.99 per month or $239.88 per year, and it stays open through December 31, 2026. Everything below explains what you are joining, and why I am asking.

The Doors Are Now Open

On September 1, 2026 we opened the doors.

Not with a webinar. Not with a panel talking at you for an hour while you quietly wondered whether anyone would notice if you slipped away to refill your coffee.

We opened with an Ask Us Anything. Questions. Frustrations. Ideas. Lived experience. And when the hour ended, the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion was live.

The building is finished. The belonging starts now.

Missed it? You can watch and listen to the full launch conversation here, with the complete transcript.

I want to be direct about what I am asking of you.

This is not a request to stand on the sidelines and cheer us on.

It is an invitation to jump in with both feet and help us build a powerful force for social justice, inclusion, equal opportunity, belonging, and human dignity for all.

Across the country, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and belonging programs are being dismantled. Funding is disappearing. People committed to this work are facing pressure, isolation, exhaustion, and fear of backlash.

We have a choice.

We can retreat into our separate corners, or we can join forces and fight back.

I choose together.

What the Coalition Is

Our purpose fits in one sentence, and we mean every word of it:

The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion helps members move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power.

And our reason for existing is simpler still:

We believe in fairness, inclusion, equal opportunity, and human dignity for all.

Four words describe how it works.

Connect. Learn. Act. Together.

Who It Is For

Whether you use the term DEI or not, if you believe every person deserves dignity, opportunity, belonging, fairness, accessibility, and the chance to thrive, this Coalition is being built for you.

Everybody.

People with disabilities. Veterans. LGBTQ+ people. Women. People of every race and ethnicity. Rural communities. Faith communities. Business leaders. Educators. Students. Parents. Nonprofit professionals. Labor leaders. Entrepreneurs. Allies. Dreamers. Builders. Neighbors.

Let me say one thing plainly, because it is what I am asked about most. Disability inclusion and accessibility are not a side room in this Coalition. There is a dedicated Accessibility and Disability Inclusion space, by design, because “everybody means everybody” is an operating principle here and not a slogan. If we do not build systems that include people with disabilities, we have not built inclusive systems at all.

What Is Actually Inside

Three things, above everything else.

BELONG. A place to exhale. Peer circles where saying “I am overwhelmed” is met with practical help rather than judgment. You are not the only one in the room. You are part of a constellation.

CLARITY. A trusted translation layer. Plain-language briefings, expert-guided sessions, and real examples of what is working right now, so you can replace guesswork and rumor with grounded confidence.

POWER. Collective strength. Shared tools, cross-sector strategy, and coalition-backed influence that turn isolated effort into coordinated, durable action.

In practice, that looks like this:

To connect, Ask the Experts office hours with seasoned practitioners, the Member Lounge, a Member Directory, Wins and Announcements, and member-led Courses and Workshops.

To learn, a growing Resource Library of articles, research, toolkits and templates, an Expand Your Perspective space, and podcasts featuring DEIAB voices.

To act, a Rapid Response Hub for the moments that will not wait, Advocacy and Engagement, Legislative and Legal Updates, DEIAB in the News, and Collaboration Projects where members build things together.

To gather, member events and a shared calendar of conferences, workshops and trainings worth your time.

Founding Membership Is Co-Authorship

This is the part I most want you to understand.

This is not early access. It is co-authorship.

This Coalition does not belong only to its founders or to established experts. It belongs to all of us, and its strength will come from all of us.

Founding Members step into the room where the blueprint is drawn. You will help design the membership tiers, the codes of conduct, the governance, the communities of practice, and the very DNA of what this becomes. You will contribute expertise, ask questions, share resources, develop projects, organize, advocate, and mentor emerging leaders.

You will carry a Founding Member designation permanently, as an architect of the Coalition. And your founding rate will never increase for as long as your membership remains active.

What It Costs

Plainly, with no small print.

Founding Member: $25.99 per month, or $239.88 per year, which works out to $19.99 a month.

Students and people who are unemployed, on the honor system: $15.99 per month, or $119.88 per year, $9.99 a month. There is no application, no paperwork, and no requirement to prove that you belong. We trust our community.

Founding Membership is open through December 31, 2026. From January 1, standard membership is $35.99 per month or $359.88 per year. You can cancel at any time, and your access runs to the end of your billing period.

How to Join, in Three Steps

  1. Go to https://community.i4sdi.org/coalition-founder.
  2. Choose monthly or annual, or the honor-system option if that is right for you.
  3. Download the app and take the Coalition with you, the DEIAB Community Coalition app for iPhone and iPad, or the DEIAB Community Coalition app on Google Play. It works just as well in a browser on your desktop.

Save the Date

Please join us for the in-person Launch Celebration of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion:

Wednesday, October 21, 2026
5:30 – 7:30 p.m.
Parkview Event Space, Sanctuary Room
200 8th Avenue North, Seattle, WA 98109

You will meet fellow Coalition members, DEIAB leaders, authors, speakers and members of the ISDI Board, and there will be book signings. Additional details and registration information will follow. For now, save the date for an evening of community, connection, celebration, and joy.

If You Want to Do More

Membership is the most important way to help build and sustain the Coalition. If you would also like to make a tax-deductible contribution, our GoFundMe campaign supports the online community, the mobile apps, accessibility, programming, and the resources available to members.

You can also learn more about the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, which created and sustains this work.

But above all, please join us.

A Joyous Rebellion

When you join, you are not simply purchasing access to another online platform. You are helping create a home for courageous conversation, practical learning, mutual support, advocacy, collective action, and the relationships that make lasting change possible.

I want this Coalition to become a joyous rebellion.

A rebellion against fear.

Against isolation.

Against division.

Against hate.

Against the idea that some of us must lose for others to belong.

Imagine people from every walk of life, across race, disability, gender, generation, affectional orientation, culture, profession, geography, identity and lived experience, standing shoulder to shoulder and declaring:

We will not retreat. We will not be divided. We will build something better. Together.

Do not wait for someone else to defend inclusion, belonging, equal opportunity, and human dignity.

This is our moment. We are the people we have been waiting for.

Become a Founding Member, invite someone you care about, and help us build a community powerful enough to meet this moment.

RESIST fear.

RESIST division.

RESIST isolation.

RESIST hate.

And together, BUILD what comes next.

RESIST. JOIN. BELONG. BUILD THE FUTURE.

With Gratitude, Intention, and Determination,

item.content:encoded:
Register today for the virtual launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion and invite someone who should not have to do this work alone.

Tuesday, September 1st

11:00 a.m. to noon Pacific / 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. Eastern

We will gather online for:

RESIST! Join the Launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion

The event is free. Learn more and register here:

https://drkirkadams.com/join-the-launch-of-the-ccsdi/

September is a season of turning.

Summer begins to loosen its warm embrace. Students return to classrooms. Families settle into new routines. Morning air grows crisp. Leaves begin trading green for gold, crimson, and copper, reminding us that transformation can be both beautiful and necessary.

To everything, there is a season.

This is our season to come together.

This is our season to turn isolation into connection, fear into courage, exhaustion into renewed purpose, and individual effort into collective power.

This is the season for the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion.

When You Feel Like the Only One in the Room

Across the country, champions of diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, belonging, human rights, and human dignity are facing intense pressure.

Programs are being dismantled. Funding is disappearing. Language is being censored. People are being asked to abandon commitments that were never merely fashionable initiatives; they were promises of fairness, opportunity, dignity, and belonging.

In workplaces, schools, nonprofits, government agencies, and communities, many champions feel like the only one in the room.

Perhaps you know that feeling.

You raise the question no one else will ask. You identify the barrier everyone else has learned to ignore. You advocate for the person whose experience is missing from the conversation. You continue speaking even when the room becomes uncomfortable.

Then you go home wondering: Is anyone else out there? Does anyone understand how exhausting this is? How long can I keep carrying it alone?

You are not alone.

But too often, the people who share our values remain separated by geography, profession, identity, institution, or issue. We may be fighting similar battles without knowing one another exists.

That isolation is not simply painful. It weakens our ability to create change.

The forces working against inclusion triumph when we are exhausted, fragmented, and afraid. Our answer must be courageous connection.

From Isolated Survival to Collective Power

The purpose of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion is clear:

The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion empowers members to move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power through courageous communication and connected communities.

And our “why” is equally clear:

We believe in fairness, inclusion, equal opportunity, and human dignity for all.

The Coalition is being created to help people address real-world issues, not simply discuss inspiring ideas.

It will be a place where champions can find practical resources, exchange strategies, learn from subject-matter experts, ask difficult questions, develop solutions, and organize collective action.

We will facilitate mentoring and peer-learning circles so people can support one another across generations, professions, identities, and experiences.

Coalition members will be able to gather in spaces devoted to the issues they care about most. They will meet people confronting similar challenges, engage with experts who can help them move forward, and contribute their own wisdom to others.

Because expertise does not come only from titles, degrees, or institutions.

Each of us carries knowledge shaped by our lived experiences. Each of us possesses a unique combination of gifts, skills, relationships, and perspectives. Something you have learned may be exactly what another person needs to take their next step.

The Coalition will create a space where we can bestow those gifts upon one another.

That is how community becomes power.

A Joyous Rebellion

Our launch is an act of resistance, but we are not building a community fueled only by anger or fear.

We are creating a joyous rebellion.

A rebellion against isolation.

Against division.

Against hopelessness.

Against the lie that expanding opportunity for one group must diminish another.

Against the idea that fairness, inclusion, accessibility, belonging, and human dignity are somehow too dangerous to name.

We will resist with courage and creativity.

We will resist with authenticity and love.

We will resist by forming relationships strong enough to carry us through difficult seasons.

Imagine people from every walk of life: across race, disability, gender, affectional orientation, generation, profession, geography, faith, identity, and lived experience, standing shoulder to shoulder and declaring:

We will not retreat. We will not be divided. We will build something better. Together.

Not Another Webinar

Our September 1 launch will not be another webinar where people talk at you for an hour while you quietly wonder whether anyone would notice if you wandered off to refill your coffee.

We are creating an Ask Us Anything conversation.

Bring your questions.

Bring your frustrations.

Bring your ideas.

Bring your lived experience.

Bring your hope, even if it is feeling a little bruised.

I will be joined by ISDI board members and community advisors representing a rich variety of backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives. We will discuss why the Coalition is needed, what members will find inside it, and how we can transform courageous conversation into meaningful action.

Most importantly, we want to hear from you.

What challenges are you facing? What resources do you need? What knowledge can you share? What could become possible if you no longer had to stand alone?

Bring Someone with You

Register for the September 1 launch and then invite someone else.

Invite the person who keeps speaking up in difficult meetings.

Invite the educator helping every student feel seen.

Invite the disability advocate demanding access.

Invite the human-resources professional trying to protect inclusive practices.

Invite the employee-resource-group leader holding people together.

Invite the executive, organizer, activist, student, neighbor, colleague, or family member who believes human dignity is worth defending.

A new season is approaching, carrying both uncertainty and possibility.

We cannot control every change the wind may bring. But we can decide how we will meet it and who will stand beside us when it arrives.

Help Us Build What Comes Next

You can also help bring the Coalition to life by supporting our GoFundMe campaign.

Every contribution, whether it is $10, $25, $50, $100, or more, helps us build and sustain the Coalition’s online community and mobile apps. If you are unable to give right now, sharing the campaign with your networks can be an equally powerful act of support.

Support and share our GoFundMe campaign:

https://gofundme.com/f/support-our-fight-for-inclusion-human-dignity-for-all

Register now for the free September 1 virtual launch:

https://drkirkadams.com/join-the-launch-of-the-ccsdi/

Make a gift. Register for the launch. Share both invitations. And bring someone with you.

The leaves are turning.

The seasons are changing.

And so are we.

RESIST fear.

RESIST division.

RESIST isolation.

RESIST hate.

Together, let us build what comes next.

This is our moment. This is our community. This is our season.

item.title: Braille Is Beautiful, and Braille Is Literacy
item.dc:creator: Aaron Di Blasi

item.content:encoded:
Six small dots can hold a word, a future, and a world.

I learned to read and write braille in first grade at the Oregon State School for the Blind, after my retinas detached when I was in kindergarten. My teacher, Mrs. Summers, may she rest in peace, gave me far more than a code. She gave me literacy. She gave me privacy, independence, and a lifeline.

During long hospital stays after numerous eye surgeries, braille connected me to stories, ideas, schoolwork, and a future I could begin to imagine. Under my fingertips, fear did not get the last word. Words did.

That is why I say this without hesitation: braille is beautiful. It is beautiful not because it is quaint, nostalgic, or inspirational, but because it is language made tangible. It gives blind people direct command of spelling, punctuation, grammar, mathematics, music, formatting, and the quiet intimacy of reading for ourselves.

Listening Is Valuable. It Is Not the Same as Reading.

I love audiobooks and screen readers. Technology has opened extraordinary doors, and blind people should have access to every useful tool. But listening and reading are different cognitive and practical acts. Speech can tell me what a sentence says. Braille lets me examine how it is written. It lets me check a name, study punctuation, scan a list, edit a document, read a speech silently, label medication, take notes in a meeting, and encounter the architecture of written language.

Sighted children are not told that audiobooks make print unnecessary. Blind children should not be told that synthetic speech makes braille optional. The right principle is not braille or technology. It is braille and technology, chosen according to the task and the person.

Braille equals literacy for blind people who read through touch. Treating it as an enrichment activity rather than a core literacy medium is the educational equivalent of handing a sighted child headphones and deciding that print no longer matters.

The Famous “10 Percent” Statistic Needs a Fact-Check

For years, advocates, journalists, agencies, and even scholarly publications have repeated some version of this claim: only 10 percent of blind people read braille. The number is memorable. It is also not supported by a current, nationally representative measure of braille literacy.

A 2022 systematic review, “How Many Braille Readers? Policy, Politics, and Perception,” traced the familiar 10 percent figure largely to two sources: a 1979 National Library Service report and American Printing House for the Blind Federal Quota data. Neither was designed to measure the braille literacy rate of the entire blind population. The researchers concluded that we do not currently have sound data showing how many braille readers there are in the United States, or whether that number is rising or falling.

This does not weaken the case for braille. It strengthens the case for better research. We should stop recirculating a dramatic statistic merely because it is dramatic. Blind children and adults deserve policy grounded in fresh evidence, clear definitions, and data that distinguish fluency, functional use, primary reading medium, dual-media reading, and occasional braille use.

There is an often quoted statistic that 90% of blind adults who are employed read braille. This comes from a 1996 study by Ruby Ryles. Ryles interviewed 74 congenitally legally blind adults and compared people who had learned to read primarily through braille with those who had learned through print. Her limited but influential study found substantially better employment and reading-related outcomes among the braille group. It demonstrated an association; it did not establish the percentage of all blind Americans who read braille, and it did not prove that braille alone caused every difference.

At Last, New Global Data Are Being Gathered

An acronym I can never seem to remember is ICEVI: the International Council for Education of People with Visual Impairment. ICEVI and the World Blind Union have launched the 2026–2027 Global Braille Literacy Campaign, “More Braille: More Empowerment.” Its goals include stronger instruction, more equitable access to hard-copy and refreshable braille, technological innovation, and research into braille’s educational, social, and economic benefits.

The campaign’s Global Braille Survey is now open and seeks worldwide information about braille’s relevance, use, benefits, and barriers. It is exactly the kind of data refresh the field has needed. Braille users, families, educators, producers, and advocates should participate and share it widely.

Global Braille Survey:

https://braillists.org/survey

Campaign information:

https://icevi.org/icevi-wbu-global-braille-literacy-campaign/

A second active study, led by PhD researcher Aasha Rose, examines the relationship between braille literacy and independence, social engagement, and life satisfaction among people who learned braille.

Aasha Rose survey information:

https://braillists.org/uncategorised/braille-literacy-and-life-satisfaction-survey-by-aasha-rose/

Recent U.S. research is also filling important gaps. A 2024 workplace study reported that 66.1 percent of its 304 employed blind participants used braille on the job, while 52.6 percent used refreshable braille technology at work. This was not a population estimate, the sample consisted of employed braille users, but it is powerful evidence that braille is alive in modern workplaces. A 2025 follow-up examined factors associated with proficient braille skills.

Workplace study:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11404553/

Braille proficiency study:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12188996/

Brailled It: Blind Young People Take the Camera

This September, the documentary BRAILLED IT brings braille literacy to the big screen. The film follows blind and low-vision young people at the annual Braille Challenge, and, crucially, places cameras in their hands so they help capture their own experiences. It is not simply a film about blind youth. It is cinema shaped with and by them.

The filmmakers also treated accessibility as part of the art: the film includes open audio description and open captions in a hyperlegible font. At many tour events, audiences can meet filmmakers and advocates, experience brailling demonstrations, and participate in workshops for blind and low-vision youth.

On Sunday, September 20, 2026, I will have the honor of joining the panel discussion after the Seattle screening at the SIFF Film Center. This continues a journey that included delivering the keynote address at the 2019 Braille Challenge Gala at the University of Southern California.

I want generations of braille readers, future braille readers, families, teachers, filmmakers, and allies in that room. Strong attendance tells theater owners that authentic stories by and about blind people have an audience, and that accessible presentation should be part of cinema’s front door, not a side entrance.

Growing Braille Readers: Two Programs Worth Celebrating

NFB BELL Academy

The National Federation of the Blind’s BELL Academy, Braille Enrichment for Literacy and Learning, is a summer program for blind and low-vision children, generally ages four through twelve. Through hands-on activities, braille games, crafts, nonvisual skills, self-advocacy, and time with blind adult mentors, children build competence and confidence in community.

While serving as President and CEO of the American Foundation for the Blind and living in Arlington, VA, I had the privilege of spending the day with the blind kids and adult blind mentors at the Washington, DC BELL Academy. It was great!

In 2026, programs reached thirty-one states; registration is expected to reopen in spring 2027.

This program deserves applause. Skills grow through instruction, practice, expectation, and joy. BELL does not present braille as remediation. It presents braille as something children can own, play with, and use to build their lives.

https://nfb.org/programs-services/nfb-bell-academy

The Braille Challenge

Created by Braille Institute, the Braille Challenge is the only academic competition of its kind for blind and visually impaired students in grades one through twelve. Regional events test reading comprehension, spelling, proofreading, speed and accuracy, and tactile-graphics skills. Top students advance to international finals in Los Angeles. The 2026 finals brought fifty young readers and writers to USC, with global participation extending across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, and Kenya.

Competition is only part of its magic. For one weekend, blind young people are surrounded by peers who understand the same codes, tools, frustrations, jokes, and ambitions. Braille skill is not hidden or apologized for. It is cheered.

My wife, Daughter and I were privileged to attend this year’s closing awards ceremony and banquet.

https://brailleinstitute.org/braille-challenge/

Where Children and Adults Can Learn Braille

No single course fits everyone. Children need individualized assessment and sustained instruction from qualified teachers of students with visual impairments. Adults may learn through rehabilitation agencies, community programs, distance instruction, peer mentorship, or a combination. Useful starting points include:

Hadley offers free practical braille workshops by touch and by sight, including uncontracted and contracted braille.

https://hadleyhelps.org/workshops

The International Council on English Braille maintains a living collection of adult-learning resources for students and instructors.

https://iceb.org/adult_braille_resources-html/

Braille Institute offers free classes and services for adults, online and at Southern California centers.

https://brailleinstitute.org/find-services/adults/all-classes/

UEB Online offers free, self-paced training in Unified English Braille for sighted learners, parents, educators, and transcribers.

https://uebonline.org/

The National Library Service provides braille resources and access to downloadable and embossed braille materials through BARD for eligible U.S. readers.

https://loc.gov/nls/who-we-serve/blindness-visual-impairment/braille-resources/

In the United States, adults who are losing vision should also contact their state vocational-rehabilitation or independent-living agency. Braille is not only for children, and it is never too late to learn enough braille to label, organize, take notes, read cards, manage medication, or rediscover the pleasure of a book beneath one’s fingers.

Refreshable Braille: A Library in One Line, and a Machine with Many Tiny Moving Parts

Refreshable braille displays turn digital text into tactile characters by raising and lowering pins in braille cells. Connected to a computer or phone, or built into a notetaker, they let a reader move through email, websites, documents, code, books, and apps. Unlike speech, a display reveals exact spelling, capitalization, punctuation, spacing, and formatting. For students and professionals, that precision matters.

The promise is enormous: thousands of books can travel in one small device. The frustrations are real, too. Traditional piezoelectric braille cells are intricate and expensive. Each cell contains moving pins and actuators; dust, wear, sticky or weak pins, connectivity problems, batteries, firmware, and damaged routing buttons can interrupt access. When a display fails, a blind person may lose not a convenience but a primary channel to work or education. Repair can be slow and costly, and proprietary parts can turn a tiny mechanical failure into a very large invoice.

Prices have fallen at the low end, but access remains uneven. Affordable 20-cell devices can cost hundreds of dollars, while mainstream 40-cell displays often cost several thousand; larger devices and multiline tactile displays can cost far more. The American Foundation for the Blind’s general guide cites a range of roughly $3,500 to $15,000 for traditional displays depending on size and features, while newer models such as the Orbit family have pushed entry prices downward. Cost comparisons should always be checked against current vendor pricing.

https://aph.org/blog/blindness-history-basics-a-brief-history-of-the-refreshable-braille-display/

https://afb.org/blindness-and-low-vision/using-technology/assistive-technology-products/refreshable-braille

The future is moving beyond a single line. Devices such as the Monarch, Cadence and Dot Pad point toward multiline braille and tactile graphics, allowing readers to explore spatial layouts, charts, mathematics, and diagrams. The next frontier must include affordability, durability, repairability, interoperability, and training, not merely impressive prototypes.

Two Hundred Years Young

Louis Braille was born in France in 1809 and lost his sight after a childhood accident. As a teenager, he adapted a military night-writing system into an elegant six-dot cell. He published his first braille system in 1824, at about age fifteen. Six dots can form 64 patterns when the blank cell is included, and those patterns can represent letters, numbers, punctuation, music, mathematics, science, and much more.

Braille was initially resisted by sighted authorities, but blind readers recognized its power. That history still whispers a warning: systems should not decide what blind people need without centering blind people’s knowledge and choices. My current take on the rallying cry, “nothing about us without us!” Is, “Nothing without us!”

Braille has continued to evolve. Unified English Braille brought greater consistency to English-language literary and technical notation. Digital braille files can now move across continents in seconds. The eBraille standard promises richer, more navigable digital publications. Yet the foundational experience remains exquisitely simple: a fingertip moving across a line of raised dots, turning touch into thought.

Let the Dots Rise

Braille is not beautiful because blindness is beautiful or hardship is noble. Braille is beautiful because human beings met exclusion with invention. It is beautiful because blind people claimed the written word for ourselves.

Mrs. Summers placed that claim beneath my fingers when I was a frightened little boy. Braille stayed with me through hospital rooms, classrooms, boardrooms, speeches, books, technology, leadership, and love. It did not narrow my world. It gave my world names.

So let us retire shaky statistics and build better evidence. Let us fund teachers, families, libraries, embossers, displays, repairs, research, and innovation. Let us celebrate BELL Academy, the Braille Challenge, and every adult brave enough to place a finger on a first unfamiliar dot. Let us fill the theaters for BRAILLED IT and listen when blind young people tell their own stories.

Braille is literacy. Braille is freedom. Braille is beautiful.

And six small dots are still opening an entire world.

item.dc:creator: Dr. Kirk Adams
item.description:
Here, Dr. Kirk Adams invites readers to the free livestreamed launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, from 11:00 a.m. to noon Pacific (2:00 to 3:00 p.m. Eastern), and argues that the Coalition is inheriting a legacy rather than inventing one. Writing from a visit to Oakland in the Black Panther Party's sixtieth anniversary year, he looks past the iconography to the Party's Community Survival Programs, the free breakfasts, health clinics, sickle-cell testing, legal services and support for seniors and disabled people, and draws out the line that anchors the piece: resistance isn't only about what we stand against, it is about what we build together.

Sign up. Show up. Stand up.

On Tuesday, September 1, from 11:00 a.m. to noon Pacific / 2:00 to 3:00 p.m. Eastern, we are launching the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion with a free livestreamed event.

RESIST! Join the Launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion.

Register now:

https://www.linkedin.com/events/launch-communitycoalitionforsus7491207384133111809/

Don’t wait until September 1 to decide whether you are part of this.

You are invited now.

If you believe in fairness, inclusion, equal opportunity and human dignity for all, we need you.

If you are tired of watching diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and belonging programs being dismantled, we need you.

If you are feeling isolated, discouraged or afraid to speak up, we especially need you.

Because resistance has never been a solo act.

And neither is ours.

We Are Not Starting from Scratch

The Community Coalition will build upon, learn from, honor and respect the extraordinary work of people and movements that resisted injustice before us.

At the end of July, my wife Ros and I spent several days in Oakland, California, a city we love and where our daughter Rachel lived for many years.

Oakland is also the birthplace of the Black Panther Party, founded by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale in 1966. This year marks the Party’s 60th anniversary. (Oakland Museum of California (OMCA))

The Panthers developed an extraordinary network of what they called Community Survival Programs: free breakfasts for children, health clinics, food programs, sickle-cell testing, legal services, transportation, education, services for seniors and people with disabilities, and much more. (Black Panther History Project)

They understood something that remains profoundly relevant:

Resistance isn’t only about what we stand against. It is about what we build together.

That idea speaks directly to what we are creating with the Community Coalition.

We can resist attacks on inclusion while simultaneously building stronger communities.

We can oppose injustice while creating practical resources.

We can challenge systems while caring for the people living within them.

We can turn frustration into organization, isolation into connection and fear into collective power.

That is why our Coalition exists:

The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion empowers members to move from reactive, isolated survival mode to strategic, sustainable, collective power through courageous communication and connected communities.

When Movements Meet

There is another part of the Black Panther story that has particular meaning to me as a lifelong disability advocate.

In 1977, Judy Heumann and other disability activists occupied the federal building in San Francisco, demanding implementation of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a landmark civil-rights protection prohibiting disability discrimination.

The occupation lasted 26 days.

And the protesters could not have sustained it alone. (National Park Service)

Among them was Brad Lomax, a Black disability activist with multiple sclerosis who was also a member of the Black Panther Party. Lomax helped create a bridge between the disability-rights and Black-liberation movements. (ArcGIS StoryMaps)

The Panthers responded.

They brought food and supplies to the protesters throughout the occupation. The National Park Service reports that they provided a hot meal every day as well as supplies for additional meals. Other allies including churches, labor unions, gay activists and community organizations also stepped forward. (National Park Service)

Think about that.

People came from different communities.

They had different histories.

They faced different forms of oppression.

But they recognized something in one another.

Your struggle for dignity is connected to my struggle for dignity.

That story, captured powerfully in the documentary Crip Camp, reminds us that the movements for racial justice, disability rights, LGBTQ+ equality, economic justice, women’s rights and other struggles for human dignity have never existed in neat little boxes.

They overlap.

They intersect.

And at their most powerful, they show up for one another.

That is precisely the kind of solidarity we want to nurture through the Community Coalition.

Study Is Part of Resistance

Recently I learned about the new Seattle Black Panther Party Interpretive Center, created to preserve the history of the first authorized Black Panther chapter established outside California.

This history is not distant from our family. We are privileged to know the Dixon family. Brothers Aaron and Elmer Dixon helped establish the Seattle chapter in 1968, the first authorized Black Panther Party chapter outside California.

Our two beloved grandchildren receive pediatric care at the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center, which traces its roots to the free medical clinic established by the Seattle Panthers. It is the only one of the 13 original Black Panther-founded health clinics still operating today. Every time our grandchildren receive care there, they are benefiting from a legacy of community members who saw an unmet need and built an institution to meet it.

That legacy is also present at the Madrona–Sally Goldmark Branch of The Seattle Public Library, where Ros and I took our children to check out books. Outside the library stands Richard Beyer’s sculpture The Peaceable Kingdom. Among its figures is a panther representing the Seattle Black Panthers, whose headquarters were in the Madrona neighborhood.

These are not merely artifacts from the past. They are threads running through our family’s life: the people we know, the clinic that cares for our grandchildren, the library where we nurtured our children’s love of learning and the neighborhood we call home.

The Seattle Panthers didn’t simply protest. They built. Their work included children’s breakfast programs, medical care, food distribution, transportation, clothing drives and legal assistance. The new Center describes these programs not simply as charity, but as models of collective power and self-sufficiency. (Seattle Black Panther)

I watched a video about the Center and something seemingly small grabbed me.

They have assembled the books that appeared on the Panthers’ required reading list, marked so visitors can identify them and read what the Panthers read.

I love that.

Because movements need more than passion.

Movements need study.

Panther culture placed enormous emphasis on political education, reading, discussion and learning together. The Seattle Interpretive Center continues that tradition as a place for education, dialogue, research and organizing. (Seattle Black Panther)

Our Coalition will echo that commitment in its own way.

We are creating a research and resource library, discussion spaces, opportunities to learn from experts and places where members can wrestle together with difficult questions.

Not talking points.

Not slogans.

Learning.

Listening.

Questioning.

Growing.

Then acting.

Black August: Remember, Study, Act

There is another reason this history feels especially meaningful right now.

This is Black August.

Black August emerged from California prisons in the late 1970s as a time to remember Black freedom fighters and political prisoners and to practice reflection, study, discipline and resistance. It grew from the commemoration of figures including George and Jonathan Jackson and has expanded into a broader remembrance of Black struggles for liberation. (America’s Black Holocaust Museum)

I didn’t grow up knowing about Black August.

I learned about it years later, when Ros and I moved to Arlington, Virginia, while I was serving as president and CEO of the American Foundation for the Blind.

We began listening to Washington, D.C.’s WPFW radio. Through WPFW, we learned about Black August and began attending Black August events in the D.C. area.

I was learning again.

And that matters to me.

None of us enters this work knowing everything.

We learn from people whose histories are different from ours.

We listen.

We show up.

And when we do it well, we allow what we learn to change what we do.

Put Your Dollars Where Your Values Are

August is also National Black Business Month, established in 2004 to call attention to Black entrepreneurship and encourage support for Black-owned businesses. (Black Enterprise)

So here is another form of action available to virtually all of us:

Spend some of your dollars with Black-owned businesses this month, and keep doing it after August ends.

Where we spend money matters.

When dollars circulate through locally owned businesses, they support entrepreneurs, workers, families and neighborhoods. Supporting Black-owned businesses is therefore more than a symbolic gesture. It can become part of a circular economy of community investment, people supporting businesses that employ, purchase from, mentor, sponsor and reinvest in their communities.

Resistance can look like marching.

It can look like organizing.

It can look like studying.

It can look like mentoring an entrepreneur.

And sometimes it looks like deciding where you buy dinner.

Now It Is Our Turn

We inherit powerful examples.

Not perfect movements.

Not histories without controversy or contradiction.

But examples of human beings deciding that injustice would not have the final word.

The Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion will learn from those who came before us while building something for the realities we face now.

Our “why” is simple:

WE BELIEVE IN FAIRNESS, INCLUSION, EQUAL OPPORTUNITY AND HUMAN DIGNITY FOR ALL.

And on September 1, we begin bringing people together around that belief.

This will not be another webinar where experts talk at you for an hour.

It will be an Ask Us Anything conversation.

Bring your questions.

Bring your frustration.

Bring your ideas.

Bring your lived experience.

Bring your courage.

And bring somebody with you.

SIGN UP NOW

RESIST! Join the Launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion

Tuesday, September 1, 2026
11:00 a.m.–noon Pacific / 2:00–3:00 p.m. Eastern

Register here:

https://www.linkedin.com/events/launch-communitycoalitionforsus7491207384133111809/

And if you believe this Coalition needs to exist, please help us build it.

We are raising funds to create the Coalition’s online community and mobile app on the Circle platform. A gift of $10, $25, $50, $100, or whatever is right for you, moves us closer.

Donate:

https://gofundme.com/f/support-our-fight-for-inclusion-human-dignity-for-all

Sign up.

Make a gift.

Invite someone else.

RESIST fear.

RESIST division.

RESIST isolation.

RESIST hate.

And learn from those who resisted before us.

Because the strongest movements don’t just fight what is wrong.

They build what comes next.

Let’s build it together.
